jurisdiction: United States — federal layer only (no state law analysed; see "state-law preemption reality" below)
headline: Federal law never makes any of these four models lawful — UIGEA, the Illegal Gambling Business Act and the Travel Act are all derivative of state law and 31 U.S.C. § 5361(b) expressly disclaims preemption — so the only genuinely independent federal gates are (1) FinCEN money-transmitter registration, which Model B triggers outright and Model C triggers if you hold withdrawable user balances, (2) the federal wagering excise tax under 26 U.S.C. §§ 4401/4411, which the IRS has already applied to paid-entry skill contests regardless of skill-vs-chance, and (3) FTC Act § 5 / COPPA, where the 2026 Skillz v. Papaya judgment ($719m, undisclosed bots in "skill-based" real-money games) is the single most dangerous precedent for a duel product that fills matches with AI.

modelVerdicts.reasoning: Closed-loop cosmetic coins are not a 'bet or wager' under 31 U.S.C. § 5362(1)(A): the user stakes nothing on the outcome of 'a contest of others, a sporting event, or a game subject to chance', and receives nothing of value on any outcome. No prize of value means no lottery (no prize/chance/consideration triad), so 18 U.S.C. §§ 1301-1304 are not engaged. The Wire Act reaches only 'bets or wagers' and (per the First Circuit) only sporting events — not engaged. 18 U.S.C. § 1955 requires an underlying state gambling-law violation and a 'gambling business' — not engaged. On money transmission, the coin is NOT a convertible virtual currency: FinCEN FIN-2019-G001 § 1.3 defines CVC as virtual currency that 'either has an equivalent value as currency, or acts as a substitute for currency', and a coin that can never be redeemed for money or a prize of value is neither. Independently, the operator accepts funds only integral to the sale of its own (non-money-transmission) service and so falls in the exemption at 31 C.F.R. § 1010.100(ff)(5)(ii)(F). If instead characterised as prepaid access, a closed-loop arrangement limited to $2,000 of value per device per day is not a 'prepaid program' (FinCEN Prepaid Access Final Rule, 76 FR 45403, 26 July 2011). No FinCEN registration. Residual federal exposure is consumer-protection only: FTC Act § 5 dark-pattern liability over confusing multi-step currency conversions and purchase flows (U.S. v. Epic Games, $245m order finalised March 2023; U.S. v. Cognosphere LLC, $20m, complaint filed 17 Jan 2025, which also barred loot-box sales to under-16s without parental consent), plus COPPA. CAUTION: FinCEN states it 'interprets these exemptions strictly' (FIN-2019-G001 at 9) — the moment a single coin can be cashed out, traded between users, or redeemed for a prize with real value, Model A collapses into Model B.

modelVerdicts.reasoning: Two separate federal problems, one of which is an outright registration requirement. (1) MONEY TRANSMISSION — MANDATORY. A coin that is purchased for dollars, staked player-v-player, and redeemed for cash or prizes of value has 'an equivalent value as currency' and is therefore CVC / 'other value that substitutes for currency' (FIN-2019-G001 § 1.3). The operator issues it and has authority to redeem it, i.e. it is an 'administrator', which FinCEN says generally qualifies as a money transmitter (FIN-2019-G001 § 3, consolidating FIN-2013-G001). FIN-2019-G001 § 4.7 ('CVC Money Transmission Performed by Internet Casinos') is squarely on point and closes the escape route: 'Any person engaged in the business of gambling that is not covered by the regulatory definition of casino, gambling casino, or card club, but accepts and transmits value denominated in CVC, may still be regulated under the BSA as a money transmitter. Indeed, even when the original transmission or the payout are done on a conditional basis (that is, only if a certain event occurs), money transmission under BSA regulations still occurs at the moment the condition is satisfied.' A duel escrow is exactly that conditional transmission. The § (ff)(5)(ii)(F) 'integral' exemption is unavailable because moving value between players IS the service. Consequence: FinCEN Form 107 registration within 180 days (31 C.F.R. § 1022.380), written AML programme (31 C.F.R. § 1022.210), SAR filing (31 C.F.R. § 1022.320), recordkeeping, biennial renewal. (2) GAMBLING — DERIVATIVE BUT LIVE. Whether the duel is a 'bet or wager' under § 5362(1)(A) is genuinely unsettled: a head-to-head trivia duel is not a 'contest of others' (the staker is the contestant) and not a 'sporting event', so everything turns on whether it is 'a game subject to chance' — question draw, matchmaking and a 5-second reaction race all inject chance, but there is no federal authority on point. It largely does not matter, because UIGEA only bites where the bet is 'unlawful under any applicable Federal or State law' (§ 5362(10)(A)). Multiple states enacted express dual-currency/sweepstakes bans taking effect across 2026 (secondary sources: California 1 Jan 2026; Indiana HB 1052 eff. 1 Jul 2026; also Connecticut, Maine, Montana, New Jersey, New York, Tennessee; Oklahoma 1 Nov 2026; Louisiana 1 Aug 2026). For users in those states, accepting cards/ACH is a § 5363 violation exposing the operator to fine, up to 5 years and a permanent injunction under § 5366, and the operation becomes an 'illegal gambling business' under 18 U.S.C. § 1955 (state-law violation + 5 or more persons + 30 days or $2,000 in a single day) carrying up to 5 years plus forfeiture. (3) WIRE ACT — probably out (non-sports) under N.H. Lottery Comm'n v. Rosen, 986 F.3d 38 (1st Cir. 20 Jan. 2021), but the 2018 OLC opinion reading § 1084 to cover all wagering has never been formally rescinded by DOJ and is not binding law outside the First Circuit; residual risk is real but low given DOJ's non-enforcement posture since 2021. (4) Federal wagering excise tax applies (see Model C reasoning). Verdict: federally you cannot operate Model B without FinCEN MSB registration and a BSA/AML programme — hence 'licence-required' — and you additionally cannot operate it lawfully at all in the growing block of states that have banned the dual-currency structure. This is the highest-risk of the four models by a wide margin.

modelVerdicts.reasoning: The intended shelter is 31 U.S.C. § 5362(1)(E)(ix), and it DOES NOT WORK for trivia — this is the most commonly misread provision in the statute. Clause (ix) opens 'participation in any fantasy or simulation sports game or educational game or contest', and founders read 'educational game or contest' as a standalone carve-out. It is not: (ix) imposes three cumulative conditions, and condition (II) requires that 'All winning outcomes reflect the relative knowledge and skill of the participants and are determined predominantly by accumulated statistical results of the performance of individuals (athletes in the case of sports events) in multiple real-world sporting or other events.' A knowledge duel or expedition is not determined by accumulated statistical results of real-world events, so it fails (II) and falls outside (ix) — even though the fixed, pre-announced, entrant-count-independent prize pool satisfies condition (I) perfectly. The stronger federal argument is the threshold one: a paid-entry knowledge contest is arguably not a 'bet or wager' under § 5362(1)(A) at all, because the entrant stakes on their own performance, not on 'a contest of others', not on a sporting event, and — if outcomes are genuinely knowledge-determined — not on 'a game subject to chance'. There is no federal case law resolving this for online trivia. WIRE ACT: § 1084(a) reaches bets 'on any sporting event or contest'; the First Circuit read that phrase as a sports-limited unit (986 F.3d 38), but no other circuit has ruled and the unrescinded 2018 OLC opinion would read 'contest' broadly. IGBA/Travel Act: derivative of state law, i.e. it turns on each state's predominance / material-element / any-chance test — outside this lane. MONEY TRANSMISSION: better than Model B but design-dependent. If the announced prize pool is the operator's own money and is NOT funded by entry fees, the operator is arguably selling a service and paying its own promotional expense, so 31 C.F.R. § 1010.100(ff)(5)(ii)(F) is available — the position DFS operators take. If you hold a withdrawable cash balance for users, or the pool is entrant-funded, FIN-2019-G001 § 4.7 pulls you back toward money transmitter status. Design lever: one-way payouts, no withdrawable stored value. FEDERAL EXCISE TAX — THE UNDER-APPRECIATED KILLER: 26 U.S.C. § 4421(1)(B) defines 'wager' to include 'any wager placed in a wagering pool with respect to a sports event or a contest, if such pool is conducted for profit', and § 4421 draws no skill/chance distinction at all. In IRS Legal Advice AM 2020-009 (23 July 2020) the Office of Chief Counsel concluded a daily fantasy sports operator is liable for the § 4401 excise tax on wagers (0.25% of handle if the wager is authorised under the law of the state where accepted, 2% if not) and the § 4411 occupational tax ($50/yr authorised, $500/yr unauthorised), and must register under § 4412 — reasoning expressly that skill-vs-chance is irrelevant for federal excise purposes. The structural defence for Model C is that a FIXED, pre-announced prize not funded by entry fees is not a 'pool'. That defence is untested. AM 2020-009 is non-precedential internal advice and cannot be cited as precedent (26 U.S.C. § 6110(k)(3)), but it tells you exactly what the IRS will argue. ADVERTISING: Skillz Platform Inc. v. Papaya Gaming, Ltd., No. 1:24-cv-01646 (S.D.N.Y., Cote, J.) — April 2026 jury verdict of $420m and judgment entered 28 July 2026 awarding $719m in disgorgement plus $10.1m in fees, for marketing real-money tournaments as head-to-head skill contests while filling them with undisclosed bots. If FACT//DUEL ever matches a paying player against an AI opponent without unmissable disclosure, that is the fact pattern. Net: genuinely unsettled federally, materially safer than Model B, and the safest of the money-taking models IF the prize is operator-funded, fixed and announced, there is no withdrawable balance, and every opponent is a disclosed human or a disclosed bot.

modelVerdicts.reasoning: A recurring fee for features or cosmetics with no stake and no prize of value engages no federal gambling statute: no 'bet or wager' under 31 U.S.C. § 5362(1)(A), no lottery under 18 U.S.C. §§ 1301-1304, no 'sporting event or contest' wager under 18 U.S.C. § 1084, and nothing for 18 U.S.C. § 1955 to attach to. Not money transmission — the operator accepts funds integral to the sale of its own services (31 C.F.R. § 1010.100(ff)(5)(ii)(F)). The live federal law is consumer protection. ROSCA (Restore Online Shoppers' Confidence Act), 15 U.S.C. §§ 8401-8405, Pub. L. 111-345, requires, for any negative-option feature sold online: clear and conspicuous disclosure of all material terms before obtaining billing information, express informed consent, and simple mechanisms to stop recurring charges (§ 8403). NOTE THE 2025-2026 CHANGE — the FTC's 2024 amended Negative Option Rule (the 'click-to-cancel' rule, 16 C.F.R. Part 425) was VACATED IN ITS ENTIRETY by the Eighth Circuit in July 2025 on Magnuson-Moss procedural grounds, days before its compliance date. There is therefore currently NO FTC negative-option rule. The FTC restarted the rulemaking, submitting a draft ANPRM to OIRA on 30 January 2026 with comments due 13 April 2026, and continues to enforce aggressively under ROSCA and FTC Act § 5 in the meantime. Build the cancellation flow to click-to-cancel standards anyway: the statute still reaches deceptive or obstructive cancellation, and the rule is likely to return. Also applies: Epic Games/Cognosphere-style dark-pattern liability on the purchase flow, and COPPA if any subscriber could be under 13.

checklist.notes: This checklist is compliance research, not legal advice. The federal layer is the easy half; the state layer decides whether you can operate, and it moved substantially in 2025-2026.

risks: STATE-LAW PREEMPTION REALITY — THERE IS NONE. 31 U.S.C. § 5361(b) is an express rule of construction: 'No provision of this subchapter shall be construed as altering, limiting, or extending any Federal or State law or Tribal-State compact prohibiting, permitting, or regulating gambling' in the United States. PASPA was struck down in Murphy v. NCAA (2018), removing the only modern federal attempt to constrain state choice. UIGEA (§ 5362(10)(A)), the Illegal Gambling Business Act (18 U.S.C. § 1955(b)(1)(i)) and the Travel Act (18 U.S.C. § 1952) all take their unlawfulness FROM state law. Clearing the federal layer tells you almost nothing about whether you can operate in any given state.

THE UIGEA 'EDUCATIONAL GAME OR CONTEST' TRAP. § 5362(1)(E)(ix) reads 'participation in any fantasy or simulation sports game or educational game or contest...' and is routinely quoted as if those opening words were a self-contained carve-out for quiz products. They are not. Clause (ix) imposes three cumulative conditions, and (ix)(II) requires outcomes 'determined predominantly by accumulated statistical results of the performance of individuals ... in multiple real-world sporting or other events'. No trivia game can satisfy that. If any adviser tells the founder that FACT//DUEL is a UIGEA-exempt 'educational contest', that adviser has misread the statute.

THE FEDERAL WAGERING EXCISE TAX IS THE MOST LIKELY WAY THIS PRODUCT LOSES MONEY QUIETLY. 26 U.S.C. § 4421 makes no skill/chance distinction, and IRS Legal Advice AM 2020-009 (23 July 2020) applied §§ 4401 and 4411 to daily fantasy sports operators on exactly that basis. The 2% rate on wagers not authorised under state law is levied on HANDLE, not net revenue. A duel product with high stake velocity and a thin rake can owe more excise tax than it earns. Model this before writing a line of payments code.

MODEL A DEGRADES INTO MODEL B ON A SINGLE PRODUCT DECISION. One cash-out path, one peer-to-peer coin transfer, one 'redeem coins for a gift card' feature, or one tournament that pays a prize of value, and the coin becomes convertible virtual currency, FinCEN money-transmitter obligations attach, and the state sweepstakes bans engage. FinCEN 'interprets these exemptions strictly' (FIN-2019-G001 at 9). Put a hard architectural boundary — not a policy note — between the closed-loop coin and anything redeemable.

THE WIRE ACT IS NARROW BUT NOT SETTLED NATIONWIDE. N.H. Lottery Comm'n v. Rosen, 986 F.3d 38 (1st Cir. 20 Jan. 2021) limits 18 U.S.C. § 1084 to sporting events, and DOJ did not seek certiorari. But the 2018 OLC opinion reading § 1084 to cover all interstate wagering has never been formally withdrawn, and the First Circuit's holding binds only Maine, Massachusetts, New Hampshire, Rhode Island and Puerto Rico. In the other circuits there is no controlling authority. Treat this as low-probability, high-severity tail risk rather than a resolved question.

BOTS AND MATCHMAKING ARE NOW A NINE-FIGURE LITIGATION RISK, NOT A UX DETAIL. Skillz Platform Inc. v. Papaya Gaming, Ltd., No. 1:24-cv-01646 (S.D.N.Y., Cote, J.) produced a $420m April 2026 jury verdict and a 28 July 2026 judgment of $719m in disgorgement plus $10.1m in fees, on findings that real-money 'skill-based head-to-head' tournaments were secretly filled with bots. FACT//DUEL currently has no server and no real opponents — whatever fills a duel today must be audited and disclosed before a single dollar is staked. The claim was brought by a COMPETITOR under the Lanham Act, so this exposure exists even with no regulator interest at all.

MSB REGISTRATION IS NOT A LICENCE AND WILL NOT SATISFY THE STATES. FinCEN Form 107 is a federal registration with no approval step. It does not authorise money transmission in any state. Roughly every state requires its own money transmitter licence with bonding and net-worth requirements — a multi-year, multi-million-dollar programme that is outside this federal lane but is the real cost driver for Models B and C.

HOLDING USER BALANCES IS THE SINGLE DESIGN CHOICE THAT MOST CHANGES THE LEGAL ANSWER. A withdrawable cash balance makes the operator look like a money transmitter under 31 C.F.R. § 1010.100(ff)(5)(i)(A) even where the game itself is defensible. One-way payouts — money in, contest entered, prize paid out directly to the winner's funding instrument, no stored redeemable value — preserves the 'integral to the sale of services' exemption at § 1010.100(ff)(5)(ii)(F). This is worth designing around from day one.

headline: Model B (buy coins → stake player-v-player → redeem for cash/prizes) is unlawful as designed: roughly a dozen states criminalise wagering on contests of SKILL by statute regardless of the skill/chance debate (verified: AZ, AR, CA, DE, FL, IL, LA, MT, NV, SC, SD, plus TN/WA via chance tests), twelve more enacted express dual-currency "online sweepstakes" bans in 2025-26 that reach payment processors and affiliates as well as the operator (CA, CT, IN, IA, LA, ME, MT, NV, NJ, NY, OK, TN), and no state issues a licence for peer-to-peer trivia wagering — so there is no licensed path; Model C (fixed, pre-announced, operator-funded prize pool, operator neutral) is the only real-money design with a defensible state-law story, and even that requires geofencing about eleven states.

TWO STATE-SPECIFIC TRAPS the founder must understand, because FACT//DUEL's current design walks into them. (1) WASHINGTON: RCW 9.46.0285 defines 'thing of value' to include 'any form of credit or promise ... involving extension of a service, entertainment or a privilege of playing at a game or scheme without charge', and in Kater v. Churchill Downs Inc., 886 F.3d 784 (9th Cir. 28 Mar 2018) the Ninth Circuit held virtual casino chips were a 'thing of value' precisely because they extended play. Purchased coins that are STAKED and can be LOST therefore satisfy both the consideration and the prize elements in Washington even with zero cash-out. (2) NEW YORK: N.Y. Penal Law s.225.00(1) uses the identical formula ('extension of a service, entertainment or a privilege of playing at a game or scheme without charge'). So Model A is lawful ONLY in the strict form defined — coins bought at a fixed price and spent at a fixed price, NEVER risked on an uncertain outcome. The moment purchased coins are staked in a duel the analysis moves to Model B territory in WA and NY regardless of cash-out. FACT//DUEL today stakes its demo coins; keep purchased coins structurally separate from any staking mechanic. Residual state exposure is consumer protection (in-app purchase disclosure, minors), not gambling.

THREE INDEPENDENT KILL-SHOTS. (1) STATUTES THAT REACH SKILL WAGERING EXPRESSLY, so the trivia-is-skill argument is irrelevant: Arizona A.R.S. s.13-3301(4) defines gambling as risking value for benefit from 'a game or contest of chance OR SKILL'; California Penal Code s.337a(a)(6) criminalises laying, making, offering or accepting any bet 'upon the result ... of any trial ... or contest ... of skill, speed or power of endurance of person or animal, OR BETWEEN PERSONS'; Florida Stat. s.849.14 is titled 'Unlawful to bet on result of trial or contest of skill'; Delaware 11 Del. C. s.1403 covers registering 'bets or wagers upon the result of any trial or contest of skill, speed or power of endurance'; Illinois 720 ILCS 5/28-1(a)(1) reaches playing 'a game of chance OR SKILL for money'; Louisiana R.S. 14:90 defines gambling with no chance element at all ('any game, contest, lottery, or contrivance whereby a person risks the loss of anything of value in order to realize a profit'); Montana Code Ann. s.23-5-110 defines a lawful 'contest of skill' as one where 'the contestant is not required to pay anything of value ... to participate'; Nevada NRS 463.0152 defines a 'gambling game' as any game played 'for money ... or any representative of value' and draws no skill/chance distinction; South Dakota SDCL s.22-25A-1 defines a 'bet or wager' by reference to 'the result of a race, contest, or game' with no chance element; South Carolina S.C. Code s.16-19-40 as construed in Town of Mt. Pleasant v. Chimento (S.C. 2012) reaches games even where skill predominates; Arkansas Code s.5-66-104 reaches any device 'at which any money or property may be won or lost'. (2) CHANCE TESTS THAT CATCH A RANDOMISED TRIVIA DRAW ANYWAY: Tennessee Code s.39-17-501(1) makes it gambling where the return is 'to any degree contingent on chance'; Washington and New York, Alabama, Kentucky, Missouri, Ohio and Oregon apply a material-element test ('depends in a material degree upon an element of chance, notwithstanding that skill of the contestants may also be a factor'). Randomised question selection, a 5-second timer against an unseen opponent, and matchmaking variance are all chance inputs a prosecutor will point at. (3) EXPRESS 2025-26 DUAL-CURRENCY BANS that criminalise exactly the sweepstakes-casino structure and, critically, extend liability to payment processors, geolocation vendors, media affiliates and app-store-adjacent suppliers: California Penal Code s.337o (AB 831, eff. 1 Jan 2026, misdemeanour, $1,000-$25,000 per violation); New York Racing, Pari-Mutuel Wagering and Breeding Law s.912 (ch. 605 of 2025, signed 5 Dec 2025, immediate effect, $10,000-$100,000 per violation); New Jersey A5447 (signed 15 Aug 2025); Connecticut P.A. 25-112 / S.B. 1235 (eff. 1 Oct 2025, Class D felony); Montana S.B. 555 (eff. 1 Oct 2025); Nevada S.B. 256 (2025); Indiana H.B. 1052 / P.L. 153-2026 (signed 12 Mar 2026, eff. 1 Jul 2026, civil fines to $100,000); Maine L.D. 2007 (signed 6 Apr 2026, eff. mid-to-late Jul 2026); Iowa S.F. 2289 (signed 15 May 2026, eff. 1 Jul 2026 — cease-and-desist power over unlicensed sweepstakes gaming); Tennessee S.B. 2136 (signed 22 May 2026, immediate, enforced as a TN Consumer Protection Act violation by the AG); Louisiana H.B. 53 (Act 48) and H.B. 883 (Act 182) (eff. 1 Aug 2026, with racketeering exposure and fines to $100,000); Oklahoma S.B. 1589 (veto overridden 14 May 2026, eff. 1 Nov 2026, Class C2 felony, and its 'representative of value' definition reaches ANY dual-currency exchangeable for 'any prize, award, cash, or cash equivalent, or any chance to win'). Most of these bans require the game to 'simulate casino-style gambling', which a trivia duel arguably does not — but that gap is narrow, untested, and California's s.337a(a)(6) and Florida's s.849.14 close it independently. NO STATE LICENSES THIS. Peer-to-peer wagering on a mobile trivia app fits no existing state licence category — not casino, not sports wagering, not fantasy sports, not charitable gaming — so 'lawful-only-with-licence' is not available as an answer. Verdict: unlawful.

modelVerdicts.reasoning: A paid-entry contest of knowledge with a FIXED prize pool announced in advance, funded by the operator and NOT dependent on the number of entrants, is the strongest real-money structure available — but it is lawful in a large majority of states and flatly unlawful in a hard core, so the honest single-word answer at the 51-jurisdiction level is unsettled. THE CASE FOR IT: most states apply the dominant-factor (predominance) test, under which a contest of general knowledge is a skill contest; and many state gambling definitions carry a model-penal-code exclusion for 'bona fide contests of skill, speed, strength or endurance in which awards are made only to entrants or the owners of entries' (verified verbatim in Connecticut, Conn. Gen. Stat. s.53-278a). The single most useful authority is White v. Cuomo, 38 N.Y.3d 209 (N.Y. Ct. App., 22 Mar 2022, 4-3): New York's highest court held that Art. I s.9 of the NY Constitution 'does not encompass skill-based competitions in which participants who exercise substantial influence over the outcome of the contest are awarded PREDETERMINED FIXED PRIZES by a NEUTRAL OPERATOR'. Every element of that sentence is a design instruction: substantial player influence, predetermined fixed prizes, neutral operator. Model C satisfies it; Model B does not. THE CASE AGAINST IT: the same skill-wagering statutes listed under Model B do not care whether the prize is fixed — Arizona (skill contests are gambling by definition, and the s.13-3311 'amusement gambling intellectual contest' registration route only works for merchandise prizes under $10 with no price increment, so it is useless for cash prizes), Delaware (constitutional ban, Del. Const. art. II s.17, plus 11 Del. C. s.1403), Florida s.849.14, Louisiana R.S. 14:90 (as-a-business, no chance element), Montana s.23-5-110 (paid entry disqualifies a 'contest of skill'), South Carolina, South Dakota, Tennessee, and Washington (where RCW 9.46.240 makes transmitting gambling information over the internet a CLASS C FELONY). Nevada is a licence state with no applicable licence. Arkansas is prohibited unless the contest qualifies as a 'paid esports tournament' under Ark. Code ss.23-118-102/103 (eff. 31 Jul 2023) — a trivia app probably does not. WHAT MAKES IT WORKABLE: geofence AZ, AR, DE, FL, LA, MT, NV, SC, SD, TN, WA (and CT and IL on a conservative read — this is exactly the 9-to-12-state block list the real-money skill-gaming industry actually operates, e.g. Skillz restricts AZ, AR, CT, DE, LA, MT, SC, SD, TN); make the prize pool fixed, announced, operator-funded and entrant-count-independent; take no rake from a player-funded pot; keep the operator a non-participant; and strip randomisation out of the paid path so no material chance element exists. Then register where prize-promotion registration bites (NY GBL s.369-e over $5,000; FL Stat. s.849.094 over $5,000; RI over $500 retail; HI over $5,000). Needs a per-state opinion from gaming counsel before launch.

modelVerdicts.reasoning: A recurring fee for features or cosmetics with no stake and no prize of value engages no state gambling statute in any of the 51 jurisdictions — there is no prize, and in most states there is no risk of loss on an uncertain outcome either. The state-layer burden is consumer protection, not gaming, and it is real: roughly 25 states have automatic-renewal laws, and the 2025-26 wave tightened them. California's Automatic Renewal Law (Bus. & Prof. Code s.17600 et seq.) as amended by A.B. 2863 (signed 24 Sep 2024, eff. 1 Jul 2025) now requires express affirmative consent, covers free-to-pay conversions, requires advance notice of fee changes 7-30 days out, and mandates SAME-MEDIUM cancellation. Virginia's ARL amendments take effect 1 Jul 2026 and require an online cancel path at least as easy as sign-up. New York City's click-to-cancel rule takes effect 1 Oct 2026 and applies to subscriptions offered to NYC consumers, with New York specifically expecting an in-app cancel button. If the subscription is sold through Apple or Google, their billing and cancellation flows satisfy most of this, but the disclosure obligations still sit on the publisher. One design caution: do not let a subscription confer coins that are then STAKED — that re-imports the Model A/B analysis.

Selling via Apple/Google billing satisfies much of the cancellation mechanics but not the disclosure obligations.

checklist.issuer: Private plaintiffs' bar (and, in Kentucky, 'any other person' after six months)
checklist.cost: Exposure is uncapped: Big Fish Casino settled Kater-line claims for $155m (secondary source, widely reported)
checklist.prerequisite: Terms of service and dispute-resolution design
checklist.notes: Verified live statutes: Illinois 720 ILCS 5/28-8 (recover losses of $50+ from the winner); Kentucky KRS 372.020 (losses of $5+ recoverable; if the loser does not sue within six months, ANY OTHER PERSON may sue for TREBLE the loss); Washington RCW 4.24.070. Georgia, South Carolina, Massachusetts and Ohio have analogous statutes and were used in the 2026 prediction-market class actions against Kalshi, Robinhood and Webull (secondary: Illinois Answers Project, Mar 2026).

checklist.item: Confirm Apple App Store and Google Play real-money policy clearance before building the payment surface.
checklist.issuer: Apple; Google
checklist.cost: Store commission on any in-app purchase; nil for external real-money wallets where permitted
checklist.prerequisite: Evidence of licensure or a legal opinion, plus geo-restriction to permitted territories
checklist.notes: Both stores require real-money gaming apps to be geo-restricted to jurisdictions where the developer is licensed and to be submitted by the licensed entity. Since no state licence exists for peer-to-peer trivia wagering, Model B is very likely unshippable on both stores regardless of what state law says. Policy citation UNVERIFIED — read the current guidelines directly.

checklist.item: Commission a per-state legal opinion from gaming counsel covering all 51 jurisdictions before the first real-money launch, and a separate money-transmission opinion.
checklist.issuer: Private gaming counsel
checklist.cost: One published market data point: $15,000 for a 51-jurisdiction skill-gaming opinion (terms.law/Tokmakov advertised price). Full-service gaming firms will be materially more.
checklist.prerequisite: Frozen product spec — counsel cannot opine on a moving design
checklist.notes: Walters Law Group's published position is that 'the only reliable way to evaluate the legality of a particular skill game in the United States is to engage experienced gaming counsel to render a legal opinion' and that any blanket list of legal states is unreliable. One firm reported reaching ZERO unconditionally cleared states in a recent comprehensive engagement. Treat this checklist as a map, not an opinion.

checklist.item: Maintain a legislative watch list — this area changed materially three times in 18 months and will change again.
checklist.issuer: n/a
checklist.prerequisite: None
checklist.notes: Live pending: DC B26-0656 (Internet Gaming and Consumer Protection Act of 2026, would ban sweepstakes while legalising iGaming); Ohio HB 298; Virginia SB 579; Maryland HB 1226/HB 295/SB 652; Missouri HB 1251. Failed in 2026 but likely to return: Minnesota SF 4474/HF 4410; Florida SB 1580/HB 1467; Massachusetts H 4431; Mississippi SB 2104; Hawaii SB 3281; Texas SB 517; Arkansas SB 524. Active enforcement without legislation: Illinois Gaming Board issued 60+ cease-and-desist letters on 3 Mar 2026; Mississippi Gaming Commission C&Ds; New York AG Letitia James C&Ds to 26 platforms in Mar 2025; Kentucky AG litigation against VGW; Pennsylvania Supreme Court held in June 2026 that 'skill games' are slot machines under PA law.

subdivisions.name: Alabama
subdivisions.detail: Material-element test: a 'contest of chance' is one whose outcome 'depends in a material degree upon an element of chance, notwithstanding that skill of the contestants may also be a factor'. A skill-dominant trivia contest with no randomisation is defensible (Model C); Model B is unsettled and exposed to Alabama's gambling-loss-recovery statute, which was used in the 2026 prediction-market class actions. No sweepstakes ban enacted. Constitutional ban on lotteries (Ala. Const. art. IV s.65) is a background risk for anything pot-like.
subdivisions.authority: Ala. Code s.13A-12-20(4) ('contest of chance'), s.13A-12-21 (simple gambling) — text via FindLaw secondary. Alabama loss-recovery statute section UNVERIFIED.

subdivisions.name: Alaska
subdivisions.detail: Gambling is defined by reference to a contest of chance or a future contingent event not under the participant's control; no enacted sweepstakes ban and no express skill-wagering prohibition found. Model C plausibly permitted, Model B unsettled. Alaska has no commercial gaming regime, so there is no licence to obtain.
subdivisions.authority: AS 11.66.280 (gambling definitions) — section text UNVERIFIED in this pass.

subdivisions.name: Arizona
subdivisions.detail: THE CLEAREST PROHIBITION IN THE COUNTRY. 'Gambling' expressly includes 'one act of risking or giving something of value for the opportunity to obtain a benefit from a game or contest of chance OR SKILL'. The skill/chance debate is legislated away. The only exceptions are 'amusement gambling' — merchandise prizes under $10 wholesale, coupons capped at $550 aggregate, or an intellectual contest where the payment is part of an established purchase price with no increment added. A cash-prize trivia duel or paid-entry contest fits none of them. A.R.S. s.13-3311 provides an AG registration route for amusement-gambling intellectual contests but only inside those prize caps. Geofence. Models A and D unaffected.
subdivisions.authority: A.R.S. s.13-3301(4) (definition of 'gambling'), s.13-3301 (amusement gambling), s.13-3311 (registration, filing of rules, sworn statement, exceptions) — current Arizona Revised Statutes, azleg.gov.

subdivisions.name: Arkansas
subdivisions.detail: Broad gaming-device prohibition reaching any device 'at which any money or property may be won or lost', with no chance element required. Narrow safe harbour: paid ESPORTS tournaments are expressly not gambling if entry fees are paid in cash, prizes are disclosed in advance, and outcomes reflect the skill and performance of competitors (eff. 31 Jul 2023). A mobile trivia app is very unlikely to be an 'esports tournament' as defined. Geofence unless counsel can bring the product inside ch. 23-118. Blocked by Skillz.
subdivisions.authority: Ark. Code s.5-66-104 (gaming devices — prohibition); Ark. Code ss.23-118-101 to 23-118-103 (Paid Esports Tournaments, HB 1349 of 2023, eff. 31 Jul 2023).

subdivisions.name: California
subdivisions.detail: TWO SEPARATE PROHIBITIONS. (1) Penal Code s.337a(a)(6) criminalises laying, making, offering or accepting any bet 'upon the result, or purported result, of any trial ... or contest ... of skill, speed or power of endurance of person or animal, OR BETWEEN PERSONS' — a player-v-player trivia stake is squarely within it; subdivisions (2), (3) and (4) reach operating a place for such wagers, RECEIVING OR HOLDING the money staked, and recording the wagers. First offence up to one year and/or $5,000. (2) Penal Code s.337o (added by AB 831, signed 11 Oct 2025, eff. 1 Jan 2026) bans operating an 'online sweepstakes game' — a dual-currency internet game that simulates gambling and awards cash or cash equivalents — and extends liability to financial institutions, payment processors, geolocation providers, content suppliers and media affiliates who knowingly and willfully support it; misdemeanour, $1,000-$25,000 per violation, up to one year. A trivia duel arguably does not 'simulate gambling' for s.337o purposes, but s.337a(a)(6) closes that gap. California applies the predominance test generally (In re Allen, 59 Cal.2d 5 (1962)), so Model C with an operator-funded fixed prize and no player-v-player pot is the only structure with a case — get a California opinion.
subdivisions.authority: Cal. Penal Code s.337a(a)(2),(3),(4),(6); Cal. Penal Code s.337o (AB 831, eff. 1 Jan 2026); Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code s.17539.1 (as amended by AB 831). Regulator: California Attorney General / Department of Justice Bureau of Gambling Control.

subdivisions.name: Colorado
subdivisions.detail: Colorado's gambling definition is generally understood to exclude 'bona fide contests of skill, speed, strength or endurance in which awards are made only to entrants or the owners of entries', which would support Model C and possibly Model B. But promotions-law compliance guides list Colorado as a state that does not permit entry fees in contests. The two framings conflict and I could not resolve them from a primary source in this pass. No sweepstakes ban enacted. Treat as unresolved and get a Colorado opinion before taking paid entries.
subdivisions.authority: C.R.S. s.18-10-102 (gambling definitions) — skill-contest exclusion text UNVERIFIED. Conflicting secondary source: Sweeppea state compliance guide.

subdivisions.name: Connecticut
subdivisions.detail: Cuts both ways, so treat it as prohibited. The gambling definition DOES exclude 'legal contests of skill, speed, strength or endurance in which awards are made only to entrants or the owners of entries' (verbatim), which on its face supports Model C and even Model B. But S.B. 1235 / Public Act 25-112 (signed 11 Jun 2025, eff. 1 Oct 2025) makes operating an online sweepstakes casino a CLASS D FELONY, and the entire real-money skill industry (including Skillz) blocks Connecticut, which tells you how the Department of Consumer Protection reads the 'legal contests' circularity. Geofence unless you are willing to fund a test case.
subdivisions.authority: Conn. Gen. Stat. s.53-278a(2) (definition of 'gambling', skill-contest exclusion, 2024 revision in force); Conn. Public Act 25-112 (S.B. 1235), eff. 1 Oct 2025. Regulator: Department of Consumer Protection, Gaming Division.

subdivisions.name: Delaware
subdivisions.detail: Constitutional ban: all forms of gambling are prohibited except state-controlled lotteries, s.17B lotteries, pari-mutuel horse wagering and bingo. Separately, 'advancing gambling in the first degree' covers keeping or using any book, device or apparatus for receiving, recording or registering 'bets or wagers upon the result of any trial or contest of SKILL, speed or power of endurance of human or beast' — the 19th-century formula that catches player-v-player skill wagering explicitly. Class A misdemeanour. Blocked by Skillz. Geofence.
subdivisions.authority: Del. Const. art. II s.17 (Lotteries and Other Gambling); 11 Del. C. s.1403 (advancing gambling in the first degree); 11 Del. C. s.1401 (second degree); 11 Del. C. s.1432 (gambling definitions).

subdivisions.name: District of Columbia
subdivisions.detail: No express skill-wagering prohibition identified and no enacted sweepstakes ban, but B26-0656 (Internet Gaming and Consumer Protection Act of 2026, introduced 9 Apr 2026, under Council review as of mid-2026) would legalise regulated online gaming while banning sweepstakes casinos. DC's sporting-event definition treats esports as games of skill, which is mildly helpful for Model C. Operator-level restrictions and scrutiny already reported. Monitor closely — DC could flip within one Council period.
subdivisions.authority: D.C. Code s.22-1701 et seq. (gambling) — section text UNVERIFIED; D.C. Code s.36-601.01 (sporting events, esports as skill) via secondary source; DC Council B26-0656 (pending).

subdivisions.name: Florida
subdivisions.detail: Fla. Stat. s.849.14 is titled 'Unlawful to bet on result of trial or contest of skill, speed or power or endurance' and makes it a second-degree misdemeanour (up to 60 days, $500) to stake, bet or wager any money or thing of value on such a result. The legislature had to enact a SPECIFIC carve-out for bowling tournaments with entry fees and a purse (s.849.141), which demonstrates that entry-fee-funded prizes would otherwise be caught. Separately, s.849.094 requires filing rules and prize lists with FDACS at least 7 days out and a trust account or bond where total prize value exceeds $5,000. Florida also has no explicit agent-of-payee money-transmitter exemption. 2026 sweepstakes bills SB 1580 and HB 1467 both died. Geofence for paid play.
subdivisions.authority: Fla. Stat. s.849.14 (in force, 2025 Florida Statutes); Fla. Stat. s.849.141 (bowling exception); Fla. Stat. s.849.094 (game promotions). Regulators: Florida Attorney General; Florida Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services; Florida Gaming Control Commission.

subdivisions.name: Georgia
subdivisions.detail: No enacted sweepstakes ban and no verified skill-wagering statute, but Georgia's gambling-loss-recovery statute is live and was used in the 2026 wave of class actions against prediction-market operators and their brokers. Georgia also has an aggressive history on 'coin-operated amusement machines' with no-cash-prize rules. Model C plausibly defensible under a predominance analysis; Model B carries real private-litigation risk independent of any prosecution.
subdivisions.authority: O.C.G.A. s.16-12-21 (gambling) and s.16-12-35 (bona fide skill contest / amusement machine rules) — section text UNVERIFIED; O.C.G.A. s.13-8-3 (gambling contracts void; recovery) cited in 2026 class actions (secondary: Illinois Answers Project, Mar 2026).

subdivisions.name: Hawaii
subdivisions.detail: Hawaii has NO legal gambling of any kind — no lottery, no casinos, no sports betting — and its gambling offence tracks the model-penal-code 'contest of chance or a future contingent event not under his control' formula. SB 3281 (2026), which would have criminalised promoting illegal electronic gambling, was deferred. Promotions guides report that contests requiring an entry fee with prizes of $5,000 or more must be registered and bonded. Practically: treat Hawaii as a geofence for any paid stake, because the AG has no tolerance and there is no regulator to licence you.
subdivisions.authority: HRS s.712-1220 (gambling definitions) and s.712-1223 (gambling) — section text UNVERIFIED; Hawaii contest registration threshold from secondary promotions-law sources.

subdivisions.name: Idaho
subdivisions.detail: The Idaho Constitution bans gambling broadly and expressly prohibits 'any electronic or electromechanical imitation or simulation of any form of casino gambling'. Sweepstakes-industry trackers list Idaho alongside Washington as a state where pre-existing constitutional and statutory law already prohibits the dual-currency model without new legislation. Idaho's statutory gambling definition follows the contest-of-chance formula. Geofence Model B; Model C needs an Idaho opinion.
subdivisions.authority: Idaho Const. art. III s.20 (gambling prohibited, including simulations of casino gambling); Idaho Code s.18-3801 (gambling defined) — subsection detail UNVERIFIED.

subdivisions.name: Illinois
subdivisions.detail: Illinois criminalises playing 'a game of chance OR SKILL for money or other thing of value' — the statute names skill expressly. There is a participant-side exception for a bona fide contest for the determination of skill, speed, strength or endurance where awards are made only to entrants, but it does not shelter the OPERATOR, who remains exposed under the keeping-a-gambling-place and operating provisions. Illinois also has the most usable loss-recovery statute in the country: anyone who loses $50 or more by gambling may sue the winner in the circuit court. The Illinois Gaming Board issued cease-and-desist letters to 60+ sweepstakes operators on 3 Mar 2026. Geofence Model B; Model C needs an Illinois opinion focused on operator liability.
subdivisions.authority: 720 ILCS 5/28-1(a)(1) ('plays a game of chance or skill for money'); 720 ILCS 5/28-1(b)(2) (bona fide contest exception, participant-side); 720 ILCS 5/28-3 (keeping a gambling place); 720 ILCS 5/28-8 (loss recovery, $50 threshold). Regulator: Illinois Gaming Board; Illinois Attorney General.

subdivisions.name: Indiana
subdivisions.detail: H.B. 1052, signed 12 Mar 2026 as Public Law 153-2026, prohibits online sweepstakes games built on dual- or multi-currency systems that simulate lottery games or casino-style gaming, effective 1 Jul 2026, with civil fines up to $100,000 per violation. Operators exited the state in July 2026. Skillz separately restricts real-prize play in Indiana where playing cards are involved. A trivia duel may fall outside 'simulates lottery or casino-style gaming', but the Indiana Gaming Commission now has a fresh enforcement mandate. Geofence Model B.
subdivisions.authority: Ind. P.L. 153-2026 (H.B. 1052), signed 12 Mar 2026, eff. 1 Jul 2026; Ind. Code s.35-45-5-1 et seq. (gambling definitions) — section detail UNVERIFIED. Regulator: Indiana Gaming Commission.

subdivisions.name: Iowa
subdivisions.detail: S.F. 2289, signed by Gov. Reynolds 15 May 2026, effective 1 Jul 2026, expands the Iowa Racing and Gaming Commission's enforcement authority and expressly authorises cease-and-desist orders against operators offering games of chance, sports wagering, gambling OR SWEEPSTAKES GAMING in Iowa without a licence. Notably it does NOT define dual-currency systems or create a new criminal offence — it is a broad enforcement grant, which makes it MORE dangerous for a novel product than a narrow casino-simulation ban, because the Commission decides what counts. Iowa Code ch. 99B restricts games between individuals to bona fide social relationships. Real-money skill apps block Iowa. Geofence.
subdivisions.authority: Iowa S.F. 2289 (signed 15 May 2026, eff. 1 Jul 2026), amending Iowa Code ch. 99F; Iowa Code s.99B.12 (games between individuals). Regulator: Iowa Racing and Gaming Commission.

subdivisions.name: Kansas
subdivisions.detail: Kansas defines a 'bet' by reference to chance, with a bona fide business transaction exclusion. No enacted sweepstakes ban. Kansas historically treated daily fantasy sports as requiring legislative authorisation, which signals a restrictive AG posture toward novel paid-entry contests. Model C plausibly defensible; Model B unsettled.
subdivisions.authority: K.S.A. s.21-6403 (definitions of 'bet' and 'gambling') — section text UNVERIFIED. Regulator: Kansas Racing and Gaming Commission; Kansas Attorney General.

subdivisions.name: Kentucky
subdivisions.detail: HIGHEST PRIVATE-LITIGATION RISK IN THE UNITED STATES even though there is no sweepstakes ban. KRS 372.020 lets anyone who loses $5 or more in a 24-hour period through illegal gambling sue the WINNER for the amount lost — and if the loser does not sue within six months, 'any other person' may sue for TREBLE the value of the loss. Kentucky used this machinery to obtain a nine-figure judgment against PokerStars and the AG has active litigation against VGW. Kentucky's gambling definition uses the material-degree test, with a reported exception where results are determined solely by skill and prizes are predetermined — which, if correct, is a precise fit for Model C and a precise mismatch for Model B. Kentucky was also a venue in the 2026 prediction-market class actions. Model C: arguable. Model B: do not.
subdivisions.authority: KRS s.372.020 (loss recovery, treble damages, any-person standing); KRS s.528.010(3) (gambling, material degree) and s.528.010(5) (skill exception, predetermined prizes) — s.528.010(5) via secondary source (Legal Moves Law Firm esports guide), text UNVERIFIED. Regulator: Kentucky Attorney General.

subdivisions.name: Louisiana
subdivisions.detail: Louisiana's gambling statute has NO CHANCE ELEMENT AT ALL: gambling is 'the intentional conducting, or directly assisting in the conducting, as a business, of any game, contest, lottery, or contrivance whereby a person risks the loss of anything of value in order to realize a profit'. That definition catches a paid-entry skill contest run as a business on its face. On top of that, H.B. 53 (Act 48) and H.B. 883 (Act 182), signed 25 May 2026 and effective 1 Aug 2026, ban dual-currency online sweepstakes, treat them as 'gambling by computer', raise the maximum fine for illegal online gambling operations from $20,000 to $100,000 with up to five years, and bring racketeering exposure. Absolute geofence.
subdivisions.authority: La. R.S. 14:90 (Gambling, in force); La. Acts 2026, No. 48 (H.B. 53) and No. 182 (H.B. 883), eff. 1 Aug 2026. Regulator: Louisiana Gaming Control Board; Louisiana State Police Gaming Enforcement Division; Louisiana Attorney General.

subdivisions.name: Maine
subdivisions.detail: L.D. 2007, signed by Gov. Mills 6 Apr 2026, bans sweepstakes casinos using a dual-currency payment system that simulate casino-style gaming; effective mid-July 2026, with reports of the prohibition becoming operative 29 Jul 2026. Operators exited in July 2026. Skillz separately restricts real-prize play in Maine where playing cards are involved. Geofence Model B; Model C requires a Maine opinion.
subdivisions.authority: Me. L.D. 2007 (signed 6 Apr 2026, eff. Jul 2026); 17-A M.R.S. ch. 39 (gambling) — section detail UNVERIFIED. Regulator: Maine Gambling Control Unit.

subdivisions.name: Maryland
subdivisions.detail: Maryland has a narrow express carve-out for ESPORTS — competitions involving video games (first-person shooters, real-time strategy, MOBAs) where players compete against each other and 'the dominant element determining the results is the relative skill of the players' — with the Comptroller empowered to adopt regulations. A trivia app is not obviously within the listed genres. Maryland's general gambling provisions reach keeping or having an interest in a gaming device or place used for gambling (6 months to 1 year, $500). Promotions-law guides report that Maryland does not permit consideration in skill contests. Three 2026 sweepstakes bills (HB 1226, HB 295, SB 652) were introduced; none enacted. Unresolved — get a Maryland opinion, and consider whether the product can be characterised as an esport under s.12-114.
subdivisions.authority: Md. Code, Crim. Law s.12-114 (online fantasy competition / esports); Md. Code, Crim. Law s.12-104 (gaming devices and places); Md. Code, Com. Law s.13-305 (prizes conditioned on purchases). Regulator: Comptroller of Maryland; Maryland Lottery and Gaming Control Agency.

subdivisions.name: Massachusetts
subdivisions.detail: No enacted sweepstakes ban (H 4431, which would have legalised iGaming and banned sweepstakes, failed in the 2026 session). Massachusetts has an active AG with promulgated daily-fantasy-sports regulations, which is a useful signal that paid-entry skill contests are regulable rather than per se unlawful — but also that the AG expects to regulate them. Massachusetts was a venue in the 2026 prediction-market loss-recovery class actions. Some real-money skill apps block Massachusetts. Model C: arguable with counsel; Model B: unsettled and litigated.
subdivisions.authority: M.G.L. c.271 ss.2, 7 (gambling) — section text UNVERIFIED; 940 CMR 34.00 (AG daily fantasy sports regulations) — citation UNVERIFIED. Regulator: Massachusetts Attorney General; Massachusetts Gaming Commission.

subdivisions.name: Michigan
subdivisions.detail: Michigan's gambling provisions are generally understood to reach betting on the result of 'any contest of skill, speed or power of endurance of man or beast', the same 19th-century formula that appears in California, Florida and Delaware — but I could not verify the Michigan text in this pass. Michigan has a fully built iGaming regulator (MGCB) which has been active against unlicensed operators. No enacted sweepstakes ban. Treat as unresolved and verify MCL s.750.301 before taking paid stakes.
subdivisions.authority: MCL s.750.301 (accepting money or valuable thing contingent on an uncertain event) — text UNVERIFIED; Michigan Gaming Control and Revenue Act, MCL s.432.201 et seq. Regulator: Michigan Gaming Control Board.

subdivisions.name: Minnesota
subdivisions.detail: Minnesota's 'bet' definition is chance-based and is generally understood to exclude 'a contest of skill, speed, strength or endurance in which awards are made only to entrants or the owners of entries' — which would support both Model C and, on its face, Model B. Promotions guides nonetheless treat Minnesota cautiously. The 2026 sweepstakes bans (SF 4474 / HF 4410) failed when the session ended 18 May 2026 and will likely return. Separately relevant to Model A: Minnesota's virtual-currency customer disclosure rules under Minn. Stat. s.53B.72 took effect 1 Jan 2026.
subdivisions.authority: Minn. Stat. s.609.75 subd. 2 ('bet') and subd. 3 (exclusions, skill contests) — text UNVERIFIED; Minn. Stat. s.53B.72 (virtual currency disclosures, eff. 1 Jan 2026). Regulator: Minnesota Gambling Control Board; Minnesota Department of Commerce.

subdivisions.name: Mississippi
subdivisions.detail: No enacted sweepstakes ban — SB 2104 died in committee in 2026 — but the Mississippi Gaming Commission has issued cease-and-desist letters to sweepstakes casinos and unlicensed online operators. Mississippi's general gambling statutes are broad and the state has a full casino regulator with an enforcement appetite. Model B: geofence. Model C: Mississippi opinion needed.
subdivisions.authority: Miss. Code Ann. s.97-33-1 et seq. (gambling) — section text UNVERIFIED. Regulator: Mississippi Gaming Commission.

subdivisions.name: Missouri
subdivisions.detail: Material-element test ('contest of chance' where the outcome depends in a material degree on chance). HB 1251, modifying illegal-gambling provisions, was pending in 2026. Missouri adopted the MTMA. Model C defensible if randomisation is removed from the paid path; Model B unsettled.
subdivisions.authority: Mo. Rev. Stat. s.572.010(4) ('contest of chance') — text UNVERIFIED. Regulator: Missouri Gaming Commission; Missouri Attorney General.

subdivisions.name: Montana
subdivisions.detail: TWO INDEPENDENT PROHIBITIONS. (1) Montana defines a lawful 'contest of skill' as one in which the skill of the contestant is the predominant factor AND 'the contestant is not required to pay anything of value or purchase anything in order to participate'. Paid entry therefore disqualifies the contest from the skill exception by definition — free-to-play skill contests are fine, paid ones are not. (2) S.B. 555, effective 1 Oct 2025, amended Title 23 ch. 5 to add a definition of 'online sweepstakes gambling' capturing the dual-currency model — reportedly the first dedicated dual-currency ban in the country — with felony penalties. Absolute geofence for Models B and C. Footnote: Montana is also the ONLY state with no money transmitter licence requirement, which is irrelevant here because you cannot operate there anyway.
subdivisions.authority: Mont. Code Ann. s.23-5-110 (definition of 'contest of skill'); Mont. S.B. 555 (2025), eff. 1 Oct 2025, amending Mont. Code Ann. tit. 23 ch. 5. Regulator: Montana Department of Justice, Gambling Control Division.

subdivisions.name: Nebraska
subdivisions.detail: Nebraska's constitution restricts games of chance and the statutory gambling definition turns on an element of chance. Promotions-law compliance guides list Nebraska among states that do not permit entry fees in contests. No enacted sweepstakes ban. Unresolved — verify with a Nebraska opinion before taking paid entries.
subdivisions.authority: Neb. Const. art. III s.24; Neb. Rev. Stat. s.28-1101(4) (gambling) — text UNVERIFIED. Conflicting secondary source: Sweeppea state compliance guide. Regulator: Nebraska Department of Revenue, Charitable Gaming Division.

subdivisions.name: Nevada
subdivisions.detail: PRACTICALLY PROHIBITED. 'Game' or 'gambling game' means any game played with cards, dice, equipment or any mechanical or electronic device or machine FOR MONEY, property, checks, credit or any representative of value — the statute draws NO distinction between games of skill and games of chance. Any game that lets a player walk away with real value is a gambling game requiring a full Nevada gaming licence, and the Gaming Control Board does not recognise the dual-currency sweepstakes model as exempt. S.B. 256 (2025) added enforcement tools against unlicensed online operators including freezing earnings. There is no licence category that fits a peer-to-peer mobile trivia app, and a Nevada non-restricted licence is a multi-year, multi-million-dollar suitability process. Geofence.
subdivisions.authority: NRS s.463.0152 ('Game' and 'gambling game' defined); NRS s.463.160 (licence required); Nev. S.B. 256 (2025). Regulator: Nevada Gaming Control Board; Nevada Gaming Commission.

subdivisions.name: New Hampshire
subdivisions.detail: No enacted sweepstakes ban and no verified skill-wagering prohibition. New Hampshire has an express fantasy-sports statute, which signals that paid-entry skill contests are regulable rather than per se criminal. Model C plausibly defensible; Model B unsettled.
subdivisions.authority: RSA 647:2 (gambling) and RSA ch. 287-H (fantasy sports contests) — text UNVERIFIED. Regulator: New Hampshire Lottery Commission.

subdivisions.name: New Jersey
subdivisions.detail: Mixed, but treat Model B as prohibited. NEW JERSEY IS HELPFUL FOR MODEL C: N.J.S.A. 5:19-1 is titled 'Participation in contests of skill not deemed unlawful gambling', and New Jersey has a mature Division of Gaming Enforcement that regulates esports wagering (participants must be 18+). BUT A5447, signed 15 Aug 2025, bans most dual-currency online sweepstakes and establishes enforcement mechanisms. New Jersey is also one of the eight states with NO explicit agent-of-payee money-transmitter exemption, so the custody question is harder here. Model B: geofence. Model C: New Jersey is one of the better states, with a DGE opinion.
subdivisions.authority: N.J.S.A. 5:19-1 (contests of skill) — full text UNVERIFIED (source returned 403); N.J. A5447 (signed 15 Aug 2025); N.J.S.A. 2C:37-1 et seq. (gambling offences). Regulator: New Jersey Division of Gaming Enforcement; Casino Control Commission.

subdivisions.name: New Mexico
subdivisions.detail: New Mexico's 'bet' definition is generally understood to exclude 'a bona fide contest for the determination of skill, speed, strength or endurance in which awards are made only to entrants or the owners of entries', which would support Models B and C — but I could not verify the text. No enacted sweepstakes ban. New Mexico is one of the eight states with NO explicit agent-of-payee money-transmitter exemption. Verify before launch.
subdivisions.authority: NMSA 1978 s.30-19-1 (definitions, 'bet', bona fide contest exclusion) — text UNVERIFIED. Regulator: New Mexico Gaming Control Board.

subdivisions.name: New York
subdivisions.detail: THE MOST IMPORTANT STATE TO GET RIGHT, AND THE MOST INSTRUCTIVE. (1) MODEL B IS BANNED OUTRIGHT: Racing, Pari-Mutuel Wagering and Breeding Law s.912 (added by S5935A, ch. 605 of 2025, signed by Gov. Hochul 5 Dec 2025, EFFECTIVE IMMEDIATELY WITH NO WIND-DOWN) prohibits dual-currency online sweepstakes platforms that let players exchange game currency for cash prizes or cash equivalents and that mimic casino gaming, sports betting, lottery products or bingo — and reaches technology and game suppliers, platform providers, PAYMENT PROCESSORS AND FINANCIAL INSTITUTIONS, geolocation firms and MEDIA AFFILIATES. $10,000-$100,000 per violation plus licence revocation or ineligibility. AG Letitia James had already sent cease-and-desist letters to 26 platforms in March 2025. (2) MODEL A HAS A TRAP: Penal Law s.225.00(1) defines 'something of value' to include 'extension of a service, entertainment or a PRIVILEGE OF PLAYING AT A GAME OR SCHEME WITHOUT CHARGE' — the same wording the Ninth Circuit relied on in Kater under Washington law. A purchased coin that is staked and lost is a thing of value in New York even with no cash-out. (3) MODEL C HAS THE BEST AUTHORITY IN THE COUNTRY: White v. Cuomo, 38 N.Y.3d 209 (22 Mar 2022, 4-3), held that Art. I s.9 of the NY Constitution 'does not encompass skill-based competitions in which participants who exercise substantial influence over the outcome of the contest are awarded PREDETERMINED FIXED PRIZES by a NEUTRAL OPERATOR'. Build to that sentence. (4) Note the material-element test at Penal Law s.225.00(2) and the GBL art. 24-A s.369-e registration and bond for prize pools over $5,000 (30 days' notice, $100 fee, bond equal to total prize value).

subdivisions.name: North Carolina
subdivisions.detail: No enacted online sweepstakes ban, but North Carolina has an aggressive, litigated statute banning electronic machines and devices that conduct sweepstakes through an entertaining display, which the courts have upheld against skill-game operators. That statute is framed around machines but its reasoning is hostile to any entertaining-display-plus-prize structure. Model B: geofence. Model C: North Carolina opinion needed.

subdivisions.name: North Dakota
subdivisions.detail: Promotions-law compliance guides list North Dakota among states that do not permit entry fees in contests. No enacted sweepstakes ban and no verified skill-wagering statute. Unresolved — verify before taking paid entries.
subdivisions.authority: N.D.C.C. s.12.1-28-01 et seq. (gambling) — text UNVERIFIED. Secondary source: Sweeppea state compliance guide. Regulator: North Dakota Attorney General, Gaming Division.

subdivisions.name: Ohio
subdivisions.detail: Ohio applies a chance-weighted test ('game of chance' where the outcome is determined largely by chance) and has an active Casino Control Commission that has issued cease-and-desist letters to unlicensed operators. HB 298, which would legalise iGaming and ban sweepstakes, was pending in 2026. Ohio was a venue in the 2026 prediction-market loss-recovery class actions. Model C defensible if randomisation is stripped from the paid path; Model B unsettled and enforcement-exposed.
subdivisions.authority: O.R.C. s.2915.01(D) ('game of chance') and s.2915.02 (gambling) — text UNVERIFIED; Ohio HB 298 (pending). Regulator: Ohio Casino Control Commission; Ohio Attorney General.

subdivisions.name: Oklahoma
subdivisions.detail: S.B. 1589 — vetoed by Gov. Stitt on 7 May 2026 as 'vague and overbroad', VETO OVERRIDDEN 14 May 2026, effective 1 NOVEMBER 2026. Its definitions are the broadest of the 2026 wave: 'representative of value' means 'any and all currency used as part of a dual-currency system of payment that allows a person to exchange such currency for any prize, award, cash, or cash equivalent, OR ANY CHANCE TO WIN any prize, award, cash, or cash equivalent'. Liability extends to platform providers, payment and geolocation providers, gaming suppliers, promoters and affiliates. Class C2 felony. Oklahoma also grants tribal operators exclusive online gambling rights and is one of the eight states with no explicit agent-of-payee money-transmitter exemption. Absolute geofence for Model B.

subdivisions.name: Oregon
subdivisions.detail: Material-element test and a specific internet-gambling provision. No enacted sweepstakes ban. Oregon is one of the eight states with NO explicit agent-of-payee money-transmitter exemption, so the custody structure is harder here. Model C defensible with randomisation removed; Model B unsettled.
subdivisions.authority: ORS s.167.117(7) ('contest of chance', material degree) and ORS s.167.109 (internet gambling) — text UNVERIFIED. Regulator: Oregon Department of Justice; Oregon Lottery.

subdivisions.name: Pennsylvania
subdivisions.detail: HOSTILE TO THE 'SKILL' FRAMING. In June 2026 the Pennsylvania Supreme Court ruled that 'skill games' are slot machines under state law and must comply with the Commonwealth's gambling statutes, with enforcement stayed 120 days — making them illegal from 13 Oct 2026 unless the legislature acts. The AG obtained a $5m forfeiture and shutdown of two skill-game companies in April 2026 on felony corrupt-organisation pleas. That litigation concerns physical terminals, not online peer-to-peer contests, so it is not directly on point — but it is the clearest judicial statement anywhere that calling something a skill game does not take it out of gambling law. Pennsylvania has a full iGaming regulator. Model B: geofence. Model C: Pennsylvania opinion essential.
subdivisions.authority: 18 Pa.C.S. s.5513 (gambling devices) — text UNVERIFIED; Pennsylvania Supreme Court decision on skill games, June 2026 (case name and citation UNVERIFIED — reported by Spotlight PA). Regulator: Pennsylvania Gaming Control Board; Pennsylvania Attorney General.

subdivisions.name: Rhode Island
subdivisions.detail: No enacted sweepstakes ban and no verified skill-wagering statute, but Rhode Island has the lowest promotion-registration threshold in the country — reportedly $500 in total announced prize value for retail-linked games of chance, with no surety bond and no winners-list filing. Rhode Island is one of the eight states with NO explicit agent-of-payee money-transmitter exemption. Model C plausibly defensible; verify the registration trigger.
subdivisions.authority: R.I. Gen. Laws s.11-19-1 et seq. (gambling) — text UNVERIFIED; RI promotion registration threshold from secondary promotions-law sources. Regulator: Rhode Island Department of Business Regulation.

subdivisions.name: South Carolina
subdivisions.detail: South Carolina's unlawful-games-and-betting statute has been construed by the South Carolina Supreme Court in Town of Mt. Pleasant v. Chimento (2012) to reach games EVEN WHERE SKILL PREDOMINATES — the statutory meaning of 'gambling' in South Carolina includes games in which skill outweighs chance. H.4129 would amend the law to provide that paying a fee to play a skill-predominant game for a performance-proportionate prize is not gambling, but it has not passed. South Carolina also has a loss-recovery statute and was a venue in the 2026 prediction-market class actions. Blocked by Skillz. Absolute geofence. Footnote: South Carolina does not require a state money transmitter licence for most money-transmission activity.
subdivisions.authority: S.C. Code s.16-19-40 (unlawful games and betting); Town of Mt. Pleasant v. Chimento, 401 S.C. 522 (S.C. 2012) (citation partly UNVERIFIED); S.C. Code s.32-1-10 (loss recovery) — section UNVERIFIED; S.C. H.4129 (pending). Regulator: South Carolina Attorney General; SLED.

subdivisions.name: South Dakota
subdivisions.detail: South Dakota's internet-gambling chapter defines 'bet or wager' as taking, receiving or accepting money or any valuable thing on the understanding that it will be paid to a person if payment is contingent upon 'the result of a RACE, CONTEST, OR GAME or upon the happening of an event not known to be certain' — NO CHANCE ELEMENT IS REQUIRED, so a skill contest is squarely inside it. Establishing a location or site in the state from which to conduct a gambling business over the internet is a Class 6 FELONY (up to 2 years, $4,000), rising to Class 5 for repeat offences, and EACH INDIVIDUAL BET IS A SEPARATE VIOLATION. Blocked by Skillz. Absolute geofence. South Dakota adopted the MTMA.
subdivisions.authority: SDCL s.22-25A-1 ('bet or wager' defined); SDCL s.22-25A-8 (establishment of internet gambling business prohibited); SDCL s.22-25A-9 (each bet a separate violation). Regulator: South Dakota Commission on Gaming; South Dakota Attorney General.

subdivisions.name: Tennessee
subdivisions.detail: TWO INDEPENDENT PROHIBITIONS. (1) Tennessee defines gambling as 'risking anything of value for a profit whose return is TO ANY DEGREE CONTINGENT ON CHANCE' — effectively an any-chance test, with NO express skill exception in the definitions section. Randomised question selection alone is enough to engage it. (2) S.B. 2136, signed by Gov. Lee 22 May 2026 with IMMEDIATE EFFECT and no wind-down, prohibits online sweepstakes games using a virtual-, dual- or multi-currency system exchangeable for cash, prizes or anything of value that simulate casino-style gambling; violations are unfair or deceptive acts under the Tennessee Consumer Protection Act with AG investigative authority. The Act also targets prediction markets. Blocked by Skillz. Absolute geofence.
subdivisions.authority: Tenn. Code Ann. s.39-17-501(1) (definition of 'gambling', 2024 Tennessee Code in force); Tenn. S.B. 2136 / H.B. 1885 (signed 22 May 2026, immediate effect). Regulator: Tennessee Attorney General; Tennessee Sports Wagering Council.

subdivisions.name: Texas
subdivisions.detail: Texas criminalises making a bet on the partial or final result of a game or contest or on the performance of a participant. There is a social-gambling defence — private place, no economic benefit other than personal winnings, equal odds for all participants — but it is UNAVAILABLE TO AN OPERATOR that takes a fee or rake, which is the whole business model. SB 517 (redefining gambling devices) failed in 2026. Texas has no gaming regulator and enforcement is by district attorneys, which makes exposure unpredictable rather than absent. Model B: geofence on a conservative read. Model C: Texas opinion needed, focused on whether an operator-funded fixed prize is a 'bet'.
subdivisions.authority: Tex. Penal Code s.47.01(1) ('bet') and s.47.02 (gambling; social-gambling defence at s.47.02(b)) — text UNVERIFIED. Regulator: Texas Attorney General; local district attorneys.

subdivisions.name: Utah
subdivisions.detail: Utah is the most absolutist gambling state in the country. 'Gambling' means 'RISKING ANYTHING OF VALUE FOR A RETURN or risking anything of value upon the outcome of a contest, game, gaming scheme, or gaming device when the return or outcome is based on an element of chance' — note that the FIRST clause carries no chance qualifier at all. Combined with the constitutional prohibition, there is no lawful gambling of any kind in Utah and no regulator to licence you. Utah is also one of the eight states with NO explicit agent-of-payee money-transmitter exemption. Operator-level restrictions on sweepstakes platforms already reported. Absolute geofence for Models B and C.
subdivisions.authority: Utah Code Ann. s.76-10-1101(2) (definition of 'gambling', 2024 Utah Code in force); Utah Const. art. VI s.27. Regulator: Utah Attorney General.

subdivisions.name: Vermont
subdivisions.detail: Vermont permits persons to organise, execute or participate in contests or sweepstakes PROVIDED THAT persons who enter are NOT REQUIRED TO VENTURE MONEY OR OTHER VALUABLE THINGS. On that wording, paid entry disqualifies the contest — the same structural bar as Montana. Vermont is easy to miss because it appears on no sweepstakes-ban list. No enacted online sweepstakes ban. Geofence Models B and C pending verification.
subdivisions.authority: 13 V.S.A. s.2143b (contests and sweepstakes) — quoted text obtained from a Justia/Vermont Legislature listing summary; DIRECT FETCH FAILED, so treat the quotation as strong but RE-VERIFY before relying. 13 V.S.A. ch. 51 (gambling and lotteries). Regulator: Vermont Attorney General; Vermont Department of Liquor and Lottery.

subdivisions.name: Virginia
subdivisions.detail: Virginia's illegal-gambling definition turns on an outcome dependent on chance and is generally understood to carry an exception for a contest of speed or skill between men, animals, fowl or vehicles where participants may receive prizes — which would support Model C. Gov. Spanberger VETOED legislation to legalise electronic skill gaming devices in April 2026, and HB 161 (iGaming plus sweepstakes ban) failed in the 2026 session; SB 579 would categorise unlicensed online sweepstakes games as illegal gambling with civil penalties of $10,000-$100,000 per violation. Separately relevant to Model D: Virginia's automatic-renewal amendments take effect 1 Jul 2026, requiring an online cancel path at least as easy as sign-up. Monitor — Virginia is likely to enact a sweepstakes ban.
subdivisions.authority: Va. Code s.18.2-325 (definitions) and s.18.2-334 (exception for contests of speed or skill) — text UNVERIFIED; Va. SB 579 (2026, pending); Virginia automatic renewal law amendments eff. 1 Jul 2026 (bill number UNVERIFIED). Regulator: Virginia Lottery Board / Virginia Gaming Commission; Virginia Attorney General.

subdivisions.name: Washington
subdivisions.detail: THE MOST DANGEROUS STATE IN THE UNION FOR THIS PRODUCT, AND THE ONE THAT REACHES MODEL A. (1) Operating internet gambling — knowingly transmitting or receiving gambling information over the internet — is a CLASS C FELONY. (2) 'Thing of value' expressly includes 'any form of credit or promise ... involving extension of a service, entertainment or a privilege of playing at a game or scheme without charge'. In Kater v. Churchill Downs Inc., 886 F.3d 784 (9th Cir. 28 Mar 2018), the Ninth Circuit held Big Fish Casino's virtual chips were a 'thing of value' on exactly that basis, because without chips a user cannot play — making the free-to-play social casino illegal gambling under Washington law. The related claims settled for a reported $155m. (3) The 'contest of chance' test is material-degree, so randomised question draws are enough. (4) Washington's Recovery of Money Lost at Gambling Act gives every Washington player a private right to recover losses. (5) Sweepstakes trackers list Washington, with Idaho, as already prohibiting the dual-currency model under pre-existing law. GEOFENCE WASHINGTON FOR EVERY MODEL THAT INVOLVES STAKING PURCHASED COINS, INCLUDING MODEL A. Footnote: Washington's money-transmitter surety bond minimum is among the lowest at $10,000.

Code s.9.46.240 (internet gambling, Class C felony); s.9.46.0285 ('thing of value'); s.9.46.0237 ('gambling'); s.9.46.0225 ('contest of chance', material degree); RCW s.4.24.070 (recovery of money lost at gambling); Kater v. Churchill Downs Inc., 886 F.3d 784 (9th Cir. 2018). Regulator: Washington State Gambling Commission.

subdivisions.name: West Virginia
subdivisions.detail: No enacted sweepstakes ban and no verified skill-wagering prohibition. West Virginia has a full iGaming regulator and permits esports wagering, which signals that paid-entry skill contests are regulable rather than per se criminal. Model C plausibly defensible; Model B unsettled.
subdivisions.authority: W. Va. Code s.61-10-1 et seq. (gaming) — text UNVERIFIED. Regulator: West Virginia Lottery Commission.

subdivisions.name: Wisconsin
subdivisions.detail: Wisconsin's 'bet' definition is chance-based with exclusions for bona fide business transactions and, on the usual model-penal-code pattern, for bona fide contests of skill, speed, strength or endurance — but I could not verify the exclusion text. No enacted sweepstakes ban. Wisconsin adopted the MTMA. Model C plausibly defensible; verify before launch.

subdivisions.name: Wyoming
subdivisions.detail: Wyoming's gambling definition turns on gain 'contingent in whole or in part upon lot, chance, the operation of a gambling device' and is generally understood to exclude bona fide contests of skill, speed, strength or endurance in which awards are made only to entrants or the owners of entries — one of the more permissive framings. No enacted sweepstakes ban. Wyoming is one of the eight states with NO explicit agent-of-payee money-transmitter exemption, but its money-transmitter surety bond minimum is among the lowest at $10,000. Model C plausibly the most permissive state; verify the skill exclusion text.
