risks: THE SKILL ARGUMENT DOES NOT SAVE MODEL B. At least eleven states legislate around the skill/chance question entirely: Arizona (gambling includes contests 'of chance or skill'), California Penal Code s.337a(a)(6) (bets on contests of skill BETWEEN PERSONS), Florida s.849.14, Delaware 11 Del. C. s.1403, Illinois 720 ILCS 5/28-1(a)(1) ('game of chance or skill'), Louisiana R.S. 14:90 (no chance element at all), Montana s.23-5-110 (paid entry disqualifies a skill contest), Nevada NRS 463.0152 (no skill/chance distinction), South Dakota SDCL s.22-25A-1 (contest or game, no chance element), South Carolina (Chimento), Arkansas s.5-66-104. Any pitch deck or investor memo that says 'trivia is skill so we are fine' is wrong on the law in these states.

YOUR VENDORS GO DOWN WITH YOU. California Penal Code s.337o, New York Rac. Pari-Mut. Wag. & Breeding L. s.912 and Oklahoma S.B. 1589 all extend criminal or civil liability to payment processors, financial institutions, geolocation providers, content and technology suppliers, platform providers, promoters and MEDIA AFFILIATES who knowingly support a prohibited operator. The practical consequence is not that you get prosecuted first — it is that no reputable PSP, geolocation vendor or affiliate network will onboard you, and any that does will terminate on first notice, stranding player balances mid-contest.

PRIVATE LOSS-RECOVERY LITIGATION IS A BIGGER THREAT THAN PROSECUTION. Illinois 720 ILCS 5/28-8 (recover losses of $50+), Kentucky KRS 372.020 (losses of $5+; after six months ANY OTHER PERSON may sue for TREBLE the loss), Washington RCW 4.24.070, plus analogues in Georgia, South Carolina, Massachusetts and Ohio. These need no conviction, no regulator and no intent — just a player who lost money on an unlicensed game. The Kater line of cases settled for a reported $155m. The 2026 class actions against Kalshi, Robinhood and Webull used exactly this machinery across five states at once, funded by a litigation-finance firm.

WASHINGTON AND NEW YORK REACH MODEL A. RCW 9.46.0285 and N.Y. Penal Law s.225.00(1) both define a thing of value to include the privilege of playing a game without charge. Kater v. Churchill Downs (9th Cir. 2018) applied that to virtual chips. FACT//DUEL's existing demo-coin escrow — coins staked into escrow, winner takes the escrow — is structurally the same mechanic. If those coins ever become purchasable, the product is arguably illegal gambling in Washington with no cash-out feature at all. The fix is architectural and must be designed in now: purchased coins must be spend-only and structurally incapable of being staked.

THE 2026 LEGISLATIVE WAVE IS NOT OVER. Twelve states enacted sweepstakes or dual-currency bans between June 2025 and November 2026. Bills failed but will return in Minnesota, Florida, Massachusetts, Mississippi, Hawaii, Texas and Arkansas; bills are live in DC, Ohio, Virginia, Maryland and Missouri. A compliance posture built on today's map will be out of date within one legislative session. Budget for ongoing monitoring, and build the geofence as a configuration table, not as hard-coded logic.

MOST SWEEPSTAKES BANS REQUIRE THE GAME TO 'SIMULATE CASINO-STYLE GAMBLING', AND A TRIVIA DUEL PROBABLY DOES NOT — BUT DO NOT BUILD ON THAT GAP. It is untested, it is a question of characterisation that a hostile AG will resolve against you, Oklahoma's 'representative of value' definition is drafted broadly enough to reach any dual-currency exchangeable for any chance to win, Iowa's S.F. 2289 is a pure enforcement grant with no definitional limit at all, and California s.337a(a)(6) and Florida s.849.14 close the gap independently of any sweepstakes ban.

MONEY TRANSMISSION IS THE HIDDEN COST CENTRE. Holding player funds requires licences in 49 states plus DC. Fees $500-$10,000 per state, bonds from $10,000 to $500,000 (California scaling to $7m), tangible net worth the greater of $100,000 or 3% of assets, and 3-12 months per state (12-18+ for New York and California). The MTMA has been adopted by 31 states but Cooley is explicit that compliance 'remains a state-by-state proposition' — it harmonises standards, not licences. The only viable path for a startup is never to take custody, which means the payout mechanics must be designed around a licensed provider from day one, not retrofitted.

APP STORE POLICY MAY BE A HARDER GATE THAN STATE LAW. Both Apple and Google require real-money gaming apps to be submitted by the licensed entity and geo-restricted to licensed territories. Since no US state licence category exists for peer-to-peer mobile trivia wagering, Model B may simply be unshippable on either store regardless of how the state analysis comes out. Confirm this before spending on legal opinions.

THE PRODUCT'S CURRENT MECHANICS ARE THE WORST-CASE FACTS. A 5/7/10-second timer compresses the skill window and amplifies reaction-time variance; randomised question sets introduce a draw-luck element; Expeditions stake at three confidence tiers on rotating question sets, which reads as a wager on an uncertain outcome; and matchmaking determines your opponent. Each of those is a chance input a prosecutor or plaintiff will point to under a material-element test. If real money is ever introduced, the paid path must be redesigned: identical question sets for all entrants, no confidence-tier variance, and a fixed operator-funded prize.

NO STATE OFFERS A LICENCE FOR THIS. 'Lawful-only-with-licence' sounds like a path but is not one for Model B. The licence categories that exist are casino, sports wagering, fantasy sports, lottery, charitable gaming and (in a handful of states) esports wagering. A peer-to-peer trivia stake fits none. Nevada's NRS 463.0152 requires a licence for any game played for money and there is no product-appropriate licence to apply for, which converts 'licence-required' into 'prohibited' in practice.

COLORADO AND NEBRASKA CONFLICT: model-penal-code-derived gambling definitions appear to exclude bona fide skill contests where awards go only to entrants, but promotions-law compliance guides list both states as barring consideration in contests. I could not reconcile these from primary sources. The conflict probably reflects two different bodies of law (criminal gambling vs. consumer-protection prize-promotion rules) applying to the same facts, which would mean both are true and both must be satisfied — but that is an inference, not a verified finding.

MARYLAND CRIM. LAW s.12-114 — a secondary source (Legal Moves Law Firm) characterised this as recognising esports as lawful skill contests generally. The statutory text I read is narrower: it covers 'a competition involving video games, including first-person shooters, real-time strategy games, and multiplayer online battle arenas'. A trivia app is unlikely to qualify. Do not rely on the broader characterisation.

THE SKILLZ RESTRICTED-STATE LIST (AZ, AR, CT, DE, LA, MT, SC, SD, TN, plus ME and IN where playing cards are involved) is operator compliance practice, not law. It is strong evidence of where sophisticated counsel has drawn the line, but Skillz does NOT block Florida, Maryland, Iowa, Washington or Nevada, and other sources report that other real-money skill operators DO block Washington, Iowa, Indiana and Massachusetts. Operator lists disagree with each other. Do not treat any of them as a legal opinion.

MOST 2025-26 SWEEPSTAKES BANS REQUIRE THE GAME TO 'SIMULATE CASINO-STYLE GAMBLING' OR TO MIMIC CASINO/LOTTERY/BINGO/SPORTS-BETTING PRODUCTS. Whether a trivia duel or a paid-entry knowledge contest falls inside that language is GENUINELY UNSETTLED and has not been litigated anywhere as of 14 Sep 2026. I found no enforcement action, AG opinion or judicial decision applying a sweepstakes ban to a non-casino-style game. This is the central open question for Model B and it needs a real opinion per state, not an inference.

OKLAHOMA S.B. 1589's 'representative of value' definition appears broader than its 'online casino games' definition. Whether the broad definition can independently reach a non-casino dual-currency product, or only operates within the casino-games prohibition, is UNVERIFIED — I read the definition via trade press, not the enrolled bill.

The $500-$10,000 application range, the $10,000 (WA/WY) to $500,000 (NY) bond range, the California $7m volume-scaled bond, the greater-of-$100,000-or-3% net worth formula, and the 3-12 month / 12-18 month lead times should all be re-priced state by state from current NMLS state-specific requirements before being put in a budget.

The holding that 'skill games are slot machines' concerns physical terminals and is not directly applicable to an online peer-to-peer contest, but it is being widely cited as a general repudiation of the skill-game framing.

jurisdiction: European Union (EU-level framework + all 27 member states) — gambling/gaming licensing lane only
headline: There is no EU gambling licence and no EU gambling regulator — the Commission states flatly that "there is no sector-specific EU legislation in the field of gambling services" — so FACT//DUEL's money product must be licensed (or lawfully structured) state by state across 27 separate regimes, and Model B (dual-currency staking redeemable for cash) is effectively unlaunchable EU-wide because the US "free alternative method of entry" defence has no counterpart in EU definitions, while Model C (paid-entry knowledge contest) genuinely splits the Union: outside gambling law in DE/AT/NL/SE, licensable in IE/IT/ES/DK/MT, and flatly prohibited in FR.

modelVerdicts.reasoning: Closed-loop coins that never convert to money or prizes of value and are never staked player-v-player fail the 'prize'/'winnings' limb of every EU-27 gambling definition, and fail the 'wagering a stake' limb of the new EU-level AMLR definition. No gambling licence is needed in any member state. THREE CONDITIONS, each of which can flip the verdict: (1) the word 'entries' in the model description is load-bearing — if coins buy entry to anything with a prize of money or money's worth, Model A collapses into Model C or B and is re-analysed there; (2) if coins buy randomised rewards (loot-box/gacha), Belgium's Gaming Commission ruled in 2018 that paid virtual currency + chance + item of value is illegal gambling under the Gaming Act of 7 May 1999, and the Netherlands has taken a comparable line — this is the one place Model A can become criminal; (3) EU consumer law applies regardless of gambling law: the CPC Network's seven principles on in-game virtual currencies (adopted 21 March 2025, with coordinated enforcement opened the same day against Star Stable Entertainment AB) require real-money price display, no forced currency bundling, and respect for the withdrawal right, and the Digital Fairness Act is on the Commission's work programme for Q4 2026 with virtual currencies and loot boxes expressly in scope.

AMLR Regulation (EU) 2024/1624, Art. 2(1)(12) (OJ L, 19.6.2024) — 'gambling service' requires 'wagering a stake with monetary value'. CPC Network in-game virtual currency principles, 21 March 2025 (Commission consumer enforcement page). Belgian loot-box position: Gaming Commission 2018 ruling under the Gaming Act of 7 May 1999 — SECONDARY (academic/trade sources; the ruling text itself is UNVERIFIED).

modelVerdicts.reasoning: As a pan-EU proposition this is unlaunchable, and the reason is structural, not a matter of degree. The US sweepstakes-casino model survives because US law requires 'consideration', which a free alternative method of entry negates. No EU member state uses that gateway. The EU definitions are stake + chance + prize, and several expressly pre-empt the AMOE workaround: France, Art. L320-1 Code de la sécurité intérieure, says in terms that 'le sacrifice financier est établi dans les cas où une avance financière est exigée de la part des participants, MÊME SI UN REMBOURSEMENT ULTÉRIEUR EST RENDU POSSIBLE par le règlement du jeu'. Germany's § 3(1) GlüStV 2021 asks only whether an Entgelt is demanded for a Gewinnchance. Denmark's Spilleloven § 5 catches 'kombinationsspil' (skill + chance combined) outright. Spain's Ley 13/2011 Art. 3(a) catches money risked on uncertain outcomes 'con independencia de que predomine en ellos el grado de habilidad, destreza o pericia de los jugadores'. Ireland's Gambling Regulation Act 2024 catches 'a game of skill or chance, or partly of skill and partly of chance' where a payment is made for a prize of money or money's worth. Beyond definitions, the second wall is that in most states there is NO LICENCE CLASS THAT FITS. Germany's GGL issues permissions only for sports betting (§ 21), online poker (§ 22b), virtual slot machines (§ 22a), lotteries and horse betting — a player-v-player trivia stake is neither, so it is not merely unlicensed but unlicensable. Poland reserves online casino to the state company Totalizator Sportowy. Austria's online monopoly sits with Österreichische Lotterien until its reform lands. Cyprus prohibits online casino. Slovenia reserves most online verticals to Loterija Slovenije and Športna loterija. Belgium ties online licences to land-based venues. Where a fitting class DOES exist the verdict is licence-required, not lawful: Malta Type 3 (P2P games where the operator takes a commission), Italy under a D.Lgs. 41/2024 concession, Spain via a 'concursos' or 'otros juegos' general + singular licence, Denmark, Sweden, the Netherlands, Ireland, Portugal, Greece, Romania, Czechia, and most CEE states. Crucially, none of those licences reach beyond their own borders.

modelVerdicts.reasoning: This is the only model where the honest answer is that the EU has no single answer, and the split runs straight through the biggest markets. THREE CAMPS. Camp 1 — outside gambling law, no licence, because the statutory test is whether CHANCE PREDOMINATES: Germany (§ 3(1) GlüStV 2021 requires the win decision to depend 'ganz oder überwiegend vom Zufall'; a contest decided by intellectual performance is not Glücksspiel even with an entry fee, and § 284 StGB therefore does not bite — this is settled German practice, though my sources for the entry-fee commentary are IHK/law-firm notes, i.e. SECONDARY); Austria (GSpG 1989 § 1(1), 'ausschließlich oder vorwiegend vom Zufall'); Netherlands (Wet op de kansspelen Art. 1(1)(a) — gambling exists only where winners are determined by a chance mechanism on which participants cannot exert 'overwegende invloed'; a behendigheidsspel falls outside); Sweden (Spelinspektionen states on its own site that 'tävlingar där vinnaren utses genom ett prestationsmoment, det vill säga utan inslag av lottning eller slump' are not covered by the Gambling Act at all). Camp 2 — licence required even though skill predominates, because the statute says so: Ireland ('a game of skill or chance, or partly of skill and partly of chance' + payment + prize of money's worth); Italy (D.M. 17 settembre 2007 n. 186 regulates 'giochi di abilità a distanza con vincita in denaro' — remote skill games with cash prizes, expressly defined as games where the result depends on skill PREDOMINANTLY OVER the random element — and requires an ADM concession); Spain (Art. 3(a) Ley 13/2011 catches skill-predominant games expressly, and 'concursos' is one of the four general-licence categories alongside apuestas, rifas and otros juegos); Denmark (Spilleloven § 5 'kombinationsspil'); Malta (Skill Games Regulations S.L. 438.11, in force 24 January 2017, plus reg. 8 Gaming Authorisations Regulations — a skill game the MGA deems a 'controlled skill game' needs a Type 4 licence). Camp 3 — prohibited outright: France. Art. L320-1 CSI provides that the prohibition 'recouvre les jeux dont le fonctionnement repose sur le savoir-faire des joueurs', and the only relevant carve-out, the video-game competition regime at Arts. L321-8 to L321-11 CSI (inserted by the Loi pour une République numérique, implemented by Décret n° 2017-871 of 9 May 2017), applies only to competitions 'organisées en la présence physique des participants' — paid-entry ONLINE competitions are not carved out. THE PRODUCT-SPECIFIC KILLER: even in Camp 1, FACT//DUEL's 5/7/10-second timers on randomly drawn questions materially shift outcome determination toward chance. A German, Austrian, Dutch or Swedish regulator assessing whether skill 'predominates' will look at question randomisation, timer length and sample size per contest. One duel over a handful of 5-second questions is a far weaker skill case than a 50-question fixed-set contest. This is the single highest-leverage design variable in the whole EU analysis.

modelVerdicts.reasoning: A recurring fee for features or cosmetics, with no stake and no prize of money or money's worth, is not gambling in any of the 27. No gambling licence anywhere. ONE TRAP, and it is specific to this product: a subscription can itself constitute the 'consideration' that turns an otherwise-free contest into gambling. The MGA's own definition of fantasy sports — the archetype for controlled skill games — counts consideration 'whether in the form of a stake, A PERIODIC SUBSCRIPTION or the purchase of in-game items, WHICH PROVIDES AN ADVANTAGE TO THE PLAYER'. So if the FACT//DUEL subscription grants extra expedition entries, better odds, higher stake tiers, or any competitive advantage in a prize event, it becomes a paid entry and the analysis flips to Model C (or B). Keep the subscription strictly cosmetic and strictly orthogonal to any prize contest. Separately, EU consumer law bites regardless: the Digital Content Directive (EU) 2019/770, the Consumer Rights Directive's 14-day withdrawal right, and the CPC virtual-currency principles of 21 March 2025.
modelVerdicts.authority: MGA fantasy sports definition per Directive 6 of 2018 (Controlled Skill Games Ruling), 1 August 2018 — cited via MGA/Legal 500 restatement, SECONDARY. Commission CPC Network in-game virtual currency principles, 21 March 2025 (Commission page, fetched 14 Sep 2026). No gambling-law authority is engaged where there is no stake and no prize of value.

checklist.item: Accept and design around the fact that there is no EU gambling licence and no mutual recognition — budget for per-member-state licensing, not one EU authorisation
checklist.issuer: European Commission (DG GROW) / CJEU
checklist.prerequisite: None
checklist.notes: The Commission's own online gambling page states 'There is no sector-specific EU legislation in the field of gambling services' and that EU countries 'are autonomous in the way they organise their gambling services'. The CJEU confirmed in Case C-440/23 that an operator licensed in one member state has no right to serve players in a member state that prohibits the product, and that players there can recover their losses (judgment reported 16 April 2026; AG Emiliou opinion 4 September 2025). JUDGMENT DATE AND HOLDINGS ARE SECONDARY-SOURCED (trade press) — verify against curia.europa.eu before relying.

checklist.item: Decide the launch shape FIRST: Model A/D (no gambling licence anywhere) vs Model C (split 27 ways) vs Model B (do not attempt in the EU)
checklist.issuer: Founder / board decision
checklist.prerequisite: None
checklist.notes: Recommended EU sequencing: ship Model A + Model D EU-wide now with zero gambling licensing; treat Model C as a licensed-market product state by state; drop Model B for the EU entirely. The sweepstakes structure does not survive EU definitions — France's Art. L320-1 CSI expressly defeats the free-alternative-entry workaround by deeming financial sacrifice established 'même si un remboursement ultérieur est rendu possible'.

checklist.item: Geo-block France for any paid-entry contest or staking product, and geo-block it hard (IP + payment BIN + device)
checklist.issuer: ANJ (Autorité Nationale des Jeux)
checklist.prerequisite: Server-authoritative geolocation at account and transaction level
checklist.notes: Art. L320-1 CSI prohibits games 'dont le fonctionnement repose sur le savoir-faire des joueurs' where a financial sacrifice is required and any part of the gain is due to chance. The video-game competition carve-out at Arts. L321-8 to L321-11 CSI requires PHYSICAL PRESENCE of participants, so paid online contests are outside it. ANJ licences exist only for sports betting, horse betting and online poker — there is no class to apply for. France is the clearest single 'no' in the EU.

checklist.item: Geo-block or free-only in: Poland, Cyprus, Slovenia, Belgium, Austria (pending reform), Finland (until 1 July 2027) for any staking/prize product
checklist.issuer: MF Poland / National Betting Authority CY / FURS SI / Kansspelcommissie BE / BMF AT / National Police Board FI
checklist.prerequisite: Geolocation stack
checklist.notes: These are monopoly or closed-class markets where a P2P staking product cannot be licensed at all. Austria's draft reform was notified to the European Commission in August 2026 (three-month standstill) and would open multi-licensing, with unlicensed operators required to stop serving Austrian customers by 1 January 2027 to remain eligible — SECONDARY (law-firm and trade reporting). Finland's new Gambling Act was approved by the President on 16 January 2026; applications opened 1 March 2026 and the licensed market goes live 1 July 2027.

checklist.item: Establish the EU operating entity in Malta and apply to the MGA
checklist.issuer: Malta Gaming Authority (MGA); Gaming Act Cap. 583 (2018)
checklist.leadTime: UNVERIFIED — consultancies quote 4-6 months for a clean application and 6-12 months for complex ownership or novel products; the MGA publishes no service-level commitment I could verify
checklist.prerequisite: Maltese company, fit-and-proper relevant persons, business plan, system and game design documents
checklist.notes: Malta is the pragmatic establishment choice — see the 'risks' entry explaining why, and its hard limits. Fees verified from the MGA's own 'Licence Fees and Taxation' guidance note, December 2024 v3, which cites Gaming Licence Fees Regulations S.L. 583.03 and Gaming Tax Regulations S.L. 583.10.

checklist.item: Choose the MGA licence type: Type 4 (controlled skill game) if the MGA will classify a knowledge duel as one; Type 3 (P2P, operator takes commission) if it will not
checklist.issuer: Malta Gaming Authority
checklist.cost: Fixed annual licence fee: €10,000 if providing SOLELY Type 4 services; €25,000 for a B2C Gaming Service Licence otherwise (incl. Type 3). Minimum share capital: Type 4 €40,000, Type 3 €40,000, Types 1-2 €100,000
checklist.prerequisite: MGA application accepted; game design documentation demonstrating that skill determines the outcome 'alone or predominantly'
checklist.notes: MGA definitions (from the MGA's own FAQ): Type 3 = 'games of chance not played against the house and wherein the operator is not exposed to gaming risk' — player-versus-player with a commission/rake, i.e. exactly the duel-with-rake shape. Type 4 = 'controlled skill games as per regulation 8 of the Gaming Authorisations Regulations'. CRITICAL GAP: under Directive 6 of 2018 (Controlled Skill Games Ruling, 1 August 2018) FANTASY SPORTS IS THE ONLY GAME THE MGA HAS CLASSIFIED as a controlled skill game. A trivia duel would need a fresh MGA determination — budget for a pre-application ruling request. Burden of proving skill predominance is on the applicant.

checklist.item: Budget the MGA compliance contribution and the new Maltese gaming tax
checklist.issuer: MGA / Commissioner for Revenue, Malta
checklist.cost: Type 4 compliance contribution: minimum €5,000, maximum €500,000 per year; rates 0.50% on first €2m of gaming revenue, 0.75% on next €3m, 1.00% on next €5m, 1.25% on next €5m, 1.50% on next €5m, 1.75% on next €10m, 2.00% on remainder. Type 3: minimum €25,000, maximum €500,000; 4.00% on first €2m tapering to 0.40%. Gaming tax on Maltese-located players: 10% for Types 2, 3 and 4 and 15% for Type 1 from 1 October 2026 (was 5%)

checklist.prerequisite: Licence issued
checklist.notes: Compliance contribution figures verified from the MGA guidance note (Dec 2024 v3). Tax change: Gaming Tax (Amendment) Regulations 2026, Legal Notices 84 of 2026 and 86 of 2026, published 1 April 2026, in force 1 October 2026 — reported by the MGA and PwC Malta, SECONDARY as to the exact LN numbers. Start-ups qualifying under the MGA's Start-Up Undertakings Directive get a 12-month compliance-contribution moratorium.

checklist.item: Apply for a German GGL permission ONLY if the product is restructured into a licensable class — otherwise run Model C in Germany unlicensed on the skill-predominance analysis
checklist.issuer: Gemeinsame Glücksspielbehörde der Länder (GGL), Halle (Saale)
checklist.prerequisite: German legal opinion on whether chance predominates in your specific duel format
checklist.notes: GlüStV 2021 permits only sports betting (§ 21), online poker (§ 22b), virtual slot machines (§ 22a), lotteries and horse betting online. There is NO class for a P2P knowledge stake, so Model B is unlicensable in Germany, not merely unlicensed. Model C (fixed announced prize pool, entry fee, skill-determined) falls outside § 3(1) GlüStV entirely if chance does not predominate — no permission needed. GET A GERMAN OPINION ON THE 5/7/10-SECOND TIMER AND RANDOM QUESTION DRAW before relying on this. Statutory evaluation of GlüStV 2021 is due by 31 December 2026 under § 32; a successor treaty would not take effect before 2027-2028 (SECONDARY, trade press).

checklist.issuer: Dirección General de Ordenación del Juego (DGOJ), Spain
checklist.leadTime: UNVERIFIED — general licences are granted through a public convocatoria, not on demand; timing depends on the DGOJ opening a round
checklist.prerequisite: General licence must be held before the corresponding singular licence can be requested
checklist.notes: Ley 13/2011 Art. 3(a) catches money risked on uncertain outcomes 'con independencia de que predomine en ellos el grado de habilidad, destreza o pericia de los jugadores' — Spain expressly has NO pure-skill exemption. Art. 2.2 excludes only 'juegos o competiciones de puro ocio, pasatiempo o recreo que constituyan usos sociales' with no economically evaluable transfers. General licence categories: apuestas, rifas, concursos, otros juegos. DGOJ was still running a Ley 13/2011 reform consultation in July 2026 — SECONDARY.

checklist.item: Apply for an ADM concession in Italy if you want Italian players in any paid contest
checklist.issuer: Agenzia delle Dogane e dei Monopoli (ADM), Italy
checklist.leadTime: UNVERIFIED — the 2024-25 reordering tender is closed; ADM awarded 52 concessions to 46 operators in September 2025, each operator capped at 5 concessions (one domain/brand each)
checklist.prerequisite: Wait for or qualify under a future ADM bando
checklist.notes: Italy explicitly regulates skill games with cash prizes rather than exempting them: D.M. 17 settembre 2007 n. 186, 'Regolamento per la disciplina dei giochi di abilità a distanza con vincita in denaro', covers games where the result depends on player skill PREDOMINANTLY OVER the random element — so demonstrating skill predominance in Italy puts you INSIDE the licensing regime, not outside it. The remote-gaming sector was reordered by D.Lgs. 25 marzo 2024 n. 41, in force 4 April 2024. Concession award and cap figures are SECONDARY (Italian trade press reporting the ADM determina).

checklist.item: Apply for a Dutch KSA remote gambling licence if you want Model B; Model C may fall outside the Wok
checklist.issuer: Kansspelautoriteit (KSA), Netherlands
checklist.prerequisite: Dutch legal opinion on 'overwegende invloed'
checklist.notes: Wet op de kansspelen Art. 1(1)(a): gambling exists where winners are determined by a chance mechanism on which participants cannot generally exert decisive influence ('overwegende invloed'). A genuine behendigheidsspel falls outside. New licensing policy rules (Beleidsregels vergunningverlening kansspelen op afstand 2026, BVRKOA 2026) took effect 1 January 2026; the 2021 cohort of licences expires 1 October 2026 and licences run for a maximum of 5 years. Applicants must now file an exit plan and a plan for notifying the KSA of significant changes. The KSA's 2026 Toezichtagenda prioritises illegal offer and has built an alliance with payment providers, social media and hosting parties — a grey-market launch will be found.

checklist.item: Track the Irish GRAI remote gaming licence window and apply when it opens
checklist.issuer: Gambling Regulatory Authority of Ireland (GRAI)
checklist.cost: UNVERIFIED — the Gambling Regulation Act 2024 leaves fees to be prescribed by the GRAI with the Minister's consent; the pre-existing remote bookmaker regime charged €10,000 with biennial renewals of €10,000 to €200,000 by turnover (SECONDARY, A&L Goodbody guide, December 2024)
checklist.leadTime: UNVERIFIED — A&L Goodbody estimated at least 2-3 months from the Act's notice periods
checklist.prerequisite: Irish or in-scope entity; fit-and-proper declarations for every 'relevant officer' and beneficial owner; tax clearance
checklist.notes: Ireland is the most important new EU regime for this product because its definition of gaming expressly catches skill: 'games of skill or chance (or partly of skill and partly of chance) where the participant pays money for the chance to win a prize of money (or money's worth)'. Commencement order signed 3 February 2026, effective 5 February 2026; remote betting applications opened 9 February 2026; remote betting licence requirement bit from 1 July 2026; in-person from 1 December 2026. REMOTE GAMING (B2C) LICENCES ARE NOT YET OPEN — reported as Q4 2026 at earliest and possibly 2027-28; SECONDARY and inconsistent across sources. Confirm directly with the GRAI Operator Portal. Administrative sanctions reach €20m or 10% of turnover.

checklist.item: Apply for a Danish Spillemyndigheden licence for any paid contest with Danish players
checklist.issuer: Spillemyndigheden, Denmark
checklist.prerequisite: None identified
checklist.notes: Spilleloven § 5 defines 'kombinationsspil' as activities where the chance of winning depends on 'en kombination af færdighed og tilfældighed' — skill AND chance combined — and these need a licence. Only games decided purely by skill fall outside the Act. A trivia duel with randomly drawn questions is a textbook kombinationsspil. Spillemyndigheden's own public guidance is that if you charge for participation in a game or competition you must seek permission; if participation is free you need not.

checklist.item: Run the Model C skill-predominance test as a DESIGN requirement, not a legal afterthought — lengthen timers, enlarge the question set, fix the prize pool, and log the evidence
checklist.issuer: Self-imposed (evidence for DE/AT/NL/SE regulators and for an MGA Type 4 determination)
checklist.prerequisite: None
checklist.notes: The variables that decide whether chance predominates: (1) timer length — 5 seconds converts knowledge into reflex and randomness; (2) question randomisation — a random draw per duel injects chance the German/Austrian/Dutch/Swedish tests will weigh; (3) sample size — one duel over a handful of questions has high variance, a 50-question fixed set does not; (4) opponent matching — random matching adds chance, skill-banded matching removes it; (5) identical question set for all entrants in an expedition removes draw-luck entirely. Keep per-player telemetry showing that higher-knowledge players win at a rate materially above chance; this is the evidence an applicant is expected to produce, and in Malta the burden of proof is expressly on the applicant.

checklist.item: Build to the AMLR (Regulation (EU) 2024/1624) now — it applies directly from 10 July 2027 and gives the first EU-wide definition of a gambling service
checklist.issuer: National AML supervisors; Anti-Money Laundering Authority (AMLA), Frankfurt
checklist.prerequisite: Identity/KYC stack, transaction monitoring, attribution of transactions to a customer before identity verification
checklist.notes: VERIFIED PRIMARY TEXT. Art. 2(1)(12): 'gambling service' means 'a service which involves wagering a stake with monetary value in games of chance, INCLUDING THOSE WITH AN ELEMENT OF SKILL, such as lotteries, casino games, poker games and betting transactions...'. Art. 3, point (3)(g) makes providers of gambling services obliged entities. Art. 20(5) requires CDD 'upon the collection of winnings, the wagering of a stake, or both' at €2,000 or more, single or linked transactions — recital 64 confirms the threshold is met by several smaller transactions adding up. Art. 4 lets member states exempt low-risk gambling services, BUT the exemption 'shall not apply to... providers of gambling services the principal activity of which is to provide online gambling services or sport betting services'. Translation: FACT//DUEL under Model B or C cannot be exempted. This is the closest thing to an EU-level rule in this whole lane and it explicitly refuses to treat skill as a way out.

checklist.item: Comply with the CPC Network in-game virtual currency principles and prepare for the Digital Fairness Act
checklist.issuer: CPC Network (national consumer authorities, coordinated by the European Commission)
checklist.leadTime: Principles in effect since 21 March 2025; Digital Fairness Act foreseen on the Commission work programme for Q4 2026 (SECONDARY)
checklist.prerequisite: None
checklist.notes: Seven principles adopted 21 March 2025: show the real-money value of every in-game purchase, no practices that hide costs or force currency bundling, respect the withdrawal right, protect minors and vulnerable users. Coordinated enforcement was opened the same day against Star Stable Entertainment AB for direct exhortation to children, time-limited purchase pressure, and insufficient transparency about virtual-currency spending. These apply to Model A and Model D even though no gambling law does.

checklist.item: Do NOT rely on an MGA licence to reach other EU markets — it does not passport
checklist.issuer: CJEU / Malta Gaming Authority
checklist.prerequisite: None
checklist.notes: There is no mutual recognition of gaming licences in EU law. Malta's Bill 55 (2023), inserting Art. 56A into the Gaming Act, requires Maltese courts to refuse recognition of foreign judgments against MGA licensees — the Commission issued a letter of formal notice on Art. 56A, and in Case C-440/23 the CJEU confirmed that EU law does not prevent a member state prohibiting online gambling authorised elsewhere, that contracts concluded in breach of a national ban are void, and that player restitution claims are not an abuse of EU rights. Bill 55 does not shield you from a German, Dutch or Austrian claim. STATUS OF THE C-440/23 JUDGMENT IS SECONDARY-SOURCED — verify on curia.europa.eu.

checklist.item: Commission a per-market local-counsel opinion before taking money from any member state
checklist.issuer: Local gambling counsel in each target member state
checklist.prerequisite: Frozen product spec (timer, question draw, prize structure, currency flows)
checklist.notes: THIS DOCUMENT IS A COMPLIANCE CHECKLIST, NOT LEGAL ADVICE. Every Model C verdict in this analysis turns on a skill-versus-chance assessment that only a local regulator or court can settle, and the assessment is fact-specific to your exact duel format. Priority order for opinions if budget is limited: Germany (largest market, best carve-out, highest downside if wrong), Ireland (new regime, clearest capture of skill), Spain and Italy (skill expressly captured), Netherlands and Sweden (carve-out available but regulator-tested), France (confirm the geo-block, do not seek a route in).

subdivisions.name: Austria
subdivisions.detail: Model C: outside gambling law — GSpG § 1(1) captures only games where the outcome depends exclusively or predominantly on chance. Model B: cannot be licensed today; the online monopoly sits with Österreichische Lotterien. REFORM IN FLIGHT: a draft opening online gambling to multi-licensing (reportedly 20-30 licences) was notified to the European Commission in August 2026 after a consultation closing 15 July 2026; unlicensed operators serving Austrians must stop by 1 January 2027 or face an 18-month licensing exclusion (rising to 24 months from 2030). Regulator today: Bundesministerium für Finanzen / Finanzamt Österreich; a new independent authority is proposed.
subdivisions.authority: Glücksspielgesetz 1989 (GSpG) § 1(1) — TEXT UNVERIFIED this session. 2026 reform: SECONDARY (DLA Piper, Freshfields, SBC News, Aug 2026).

subdivisions.name: Belgium
subdivisions.detail: Model B: online licences are supplementary classes (A+/B+/F1+) attached to land-based establishments, so a pure-online newcomer cannot obtain one. Belgium also has the EU's most aggressive virtual-currency position: the Gaming Commission ruled in 2018 that paid loot boxes are illegal gambling because the purchase of virtual currency is a financial stake, with chance and a possibility of winning — this reaches Model A if coins buy randomised rewards. Model C: broad statutory definition; assume capture and take local advice. Regulator: Kansspelcommissie / Commission des jeux de hasard.

subdivisions.name: France
subdivisions.detail: THE CLEAREST 'NO' IN THE EU, AND IT IS SPECIFICALLY A NO TO SKILL GAMES. Art. L320-1 CSI prohibits as gambling all operations offered to the public 'pour faire naître l'espérance d'un gain qui serait dû, même partiellement, au hasard et pour lesquelles un sacrifice financier est exigé', then adds: 'Cette interdiction recouvre les jeux dont le fonctionnement repose sur le savoir-faire des joueurs. Le sacrifice financier est établi dans les cas où une avance financière est exigée de la part des participants, même si un remboursement ultérieur est rendu possible par le règlement du jeu.' That second sentence kills Model B's sweepstakes structure and the first kills Model C. The only adjacent carve-out, video-game competitions at Arts. L321-8 to L321-11 CSI (Décret n° 2017-871 of 9 May 2017), applies only where participants are PHYSICALLY PRESENT and caps entry fees at a decreed fraction of total organisation cost — paid online competitions do not qualify. ANJ licences cover only sports betting, horse betting and online poker; online casino is prohibited. Models A and D are unaffected.
subdivisions.authority: Code de la sécurité intérieure Art. L320-1, as amended by Ordonnance n° 2019-1015 du 2 octobre 2019, in force 1 January 2020; Arts. L321-8 to L321-11 CSI; Décret n° 2017-871 du 9 mai 2017; Loi n° 2010-476 du 12 mai 2010. Regulator: Autorité Nationale des Jeux (ANJ). L320-1 text obtained via search snippet of Legifrance/Lexbase — direct Legifrance fetch returned 403, so the wording is HIGH-CONFIDENCE BUT NOT DIRECTLY FETCHED.

subdivisions.name: Germany
subdivisions.detail: SPLIT BY MODEL — the largest EU market and the best-case Model C jurisdiction. § 3(1) GlüStV 2021: gambling exists where 'im Rahmen eines Spiels für den Erwerb einer Gewinnchance ein Entgelt verlangt wird und die Entscheidung über den Gewinn ganz oder überwiegend vom Zufall abhängt'. BOTH elements are needed. A contest decided by intellectual performance is therefore not Glücksspiel even with an entry fee, and § 284 StGB does not bite — Model C is lawful WITHOUT a licence. Model B is the opposite: the GGL's permission classes are exhaustive (sports betting § 21, online poker § 22b, virtual slot machines § 22a, plus lotteries and horse betting), there is no class for a player-v-player knowledge stake, so it is unlicensable rather than merely unlicensed. THE RISK: FACT//DUEL's 5/7/10-second timers on randomly drawn questions push the 'überwiegend vom Zufall' analysis toward chance. The GGL and the Länder must complete a statutory evaluation of GlüStV 2021 by 31 December 2026 (§ 32); a reformed treaty would not take effect before roughly 2027-2028.
subdivisions.authority: Staatsvertrag zur Neuregulierung des Glücksspielwesens in Deutschland (GlüStV 2021) §§ 3(1), 4, 4a, 4b, 21, 22a, 22b, 32; in force 1 July 2021, consolidated with 2022 amendments (per the GGL's own legal-basis page, fetched 14 Sep 2026). § 284 StGB. Regulator: Gemeinsame Glücksspielbehörde der Länder (GGL), Halle (Saale), operational 1 January 2023. Entry-fee/skill commentary: SECONDARY (IHK guidance notes, German law-firm notes).

subdivisions.detail: Licensing market for online betting and other online games under the 2011 framework as amended in 2019. Models B and C: assume a licence is needed. subdivisions.name: Ireland
subdivisions.detail: THE MOST CONSEQUENTIAL NEW REGIME FOR THIS PRODUCT, BECAUSE IT EXPRESSLY CAPTURES SKILL. 'Gaming' under the Gambling Regulation Act 2024 covers 'games of skill or chance (or partly of skill and partly of chance) where the participant pays money for the chance to win a prize of money (or money's worth)' — there is no skill carve-out, so Model C needs a licence just as Model B does. Lotteries are separately defined to include activities involving 'a guess of future events or of past events where the results are not generally known' — that phrasing is close enough to a trivia product to warrant specific counsel. Timeline: Act signed 23 October 2024; commencement order signed 3 February 2026 effective 5 February 2026; remote betting / remote betting intermediary / in-person betting applications opened 9 February 2026 via the GRAI Operator Portal; remote betting licence requirement from 1 July 2026; in-person from 1 December 2026. REMOTE GAMING (B2C) LICENCES ARE NOT YET OPEN — reported variously as Q4 2026 or 2027-28; confirm with the GRAI. Already in force: credit-card gambling ban, mandatory customer spending limits for remote gambling, child protection rules, suspicious-behaviour reporting. Administrative sanctions up to €20m or 10% of turnover. B2B licensing also applies to software and hosting suppliers. Exemptions are narrow: one-off charitable lotteries with prizes under €2,000, and marketing lotteries with a €5,000 prize limit.
subdivisions.authority: Gambling Regulation Act 2024 (No. 35 of 2024), s. 2 definitions; commencement order of 3 February 2026 (Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration). Regulator: Gambling Regulatory Authority of Ireland (GRAI). subdivisions.name: Italy
subdivisions.detail: ITALY DOES NOT EXEMPT SKILL — IT LICENSES IT. D.M. 17 settembre 2007 n. 186, 'Regolamento per la disciplina dei giochi di abilità a distanza con vincita in denaro', governs remote skill games with cash prizes and expressly covers games where the result depends, PREDOMINANTLY OVER the random element, on the skill of the players. ADM authorisation of both the concession and the specific game platform project is required. So proving skill predominance in Italy puts you inside the regime. The remote sector was reordered by D.Lgs. 25 marzo 2024 n. 41 (in force 4 April 2024, implementing Art. 15 of Law 111/2023); ADM ran the reordering tender and awarded 52 concessions to 46 operators in September 2025, with each operator capped at 5 concessions, one per domain and brand. Regulator: Agenzia delle Dogane e dei Monopoli (ADM).

subdivisions.name: Luxembourg
subdivisions.detail: The only EU member state with no dedicated commercial online gambling licensing regime — the Loterie Nationale operates the sanctioned offer and there is no route to licence a private online operator. That is NOT the same as permission: the absence of a licensing route usually means a private stake-and-prize product is simply unlawful rather than free. Treat as a small market not worth the analysis; if you must enter, take Luxembourg counsel.
subdivisions.authority: No dedicated online gambling regime — SECONDARY (EGBA analysis; 2026 regulators directory lists no Luxembourg entry).

subdivisions.name: Malta
subdivisions.detail: THE PRAGMATIC ESTABLISHMENT CHOICE, WITH A HARD CEILING. Malta is the only EU state with a purpose-built skill-games regime: the Skill Games Regulations (S.L. 438.11), in force 24 January 2017, define a 'skill game' as a game for money or money's worth offered by distance communication whose result is determined by skill alone or predominantly by skill; skill games the MGA considers to pose additional consumer risk are declared 'controlled skill games' and then require a Type 4 licence under reg. 8 of the Gaming Authorisations Regulations. FOR MODEL B/DUELS the likelier fit is Type 3: 'games of chance not played against the house and wherein the operator is not exposed to gaming risk' — player-v-player with a rake. THE GAP: under Directive 6 of 2018 (Controlled Skill Games Ruling, 1 August 2018) fantasy sports remains the only game the MGA has classified as a controlled skill game, so a trivia duel needs a fresh MGA determination and the burden of proving skill predominance is on the applicant. Costs (MGA's own guidance note, Dec 2024 v3): application fee €5,000; fixed annual licence fee €10,000 if providing solely Type 4, otherwise €25,000 for a B2C gaming service licence; Type 4 compliance contribution min €5,000 / max €500,000 at 0.50% rising to 2.00% by band; Type 3 min €25,000 / max €500,000 at 4.00% tapering to 0.40%; minimum share capital €40,000 for Types 3 and 4. Gaming tax applies only to players physically in Malta, and rises from 5% to 10% for Types 2-4 (15% for Type 1) from 1 October 2026. CEILING: an MGA licence does NOT passport. Bill 55 (2023) inserting Art. 56A into the Gaming Act — which requires Maltese courts to refuse recognition of foreign judgments against MGA licensees — drew a Commission letter of formal notice, and in Case C-440/23 the CJEU confirmed a member state may prohibit online gambling licensed elsewhere and that players may recover losses.
subdivisions.authority: Gaming Act (Cap. 583) 2018; Skill Games Regulations S.L. 438.11 (24 January 2017); Gaming Authorisations Regulations reg. 8; Gaming Licence Fees Regulations S.L. 583.03; Gaming Tax Regulations S.L. 583.10, amended by Gaming Tax (Amendment) Regulations 2026 (reported as LN 84/2026 and LN 86/2026, published 1 April 2026, in force 1 October 2026). MGA Directive 6 of 2018. Fee figures VERIFIED from the MGA 'Licence Fees and Taxation' guidance note, December 24 v3. Regulator: Malta Gaming Authority.

subdivisions.name: Netherlands
subdivisions.detail: Model C may fall outside the Act; Model B needs a licence. Art. 1(1)(a) Wet op de kansspelen prohibits, without a licence, giving an opportunity to compete for prizes where winners are determined by a chance mechanism on which participants generally cannot exert 'overwegende invloed' (decisive influence). A genuine behendigheidsspel is outside the Act — but Dutch courts have gone both ways on borderline cases (the Hoge Raad held poker to be a game of chance in 1998; the Hague District Court reached the opposite view in 2010), so this is not a safe harbour to assume. Current licensing: Wet Kansspelen op afstand; new policy rules BVRKOA 2026 in force 1 January 2026; the September 2021 cohort of licences expires 1 October 2026; licences run a maximum of 5 years; applicants must now submit an exit plan and a change-notification plan. The KSA's 2026 Toezichtagenda prioritises illegal supply, working through an alliance with payment service providers, social media and hosting companies.
subdivisions.authority: Wet op de kansspelen Art. 1(1)(a) — SECONDARY (KSA and law-firm restatements; statutory text not fetched). Beleidsregels vergunningverlening kansspelen op afstand 2026 (BVRKOA 2026), in force 1 January 2026 (KSA). Regulator: Kansspelautoriteit (KSA).

subdivisions.detail: Model B cannot be offered: online casino games — roulette, card games, dice games and slot machines — are a state monopoly exercised by Totalizator Sportowy, wholly owned by the State Treasury. Only mutual betting (sports betting) is open to private operators with a Ministry of Finance permit, a Polish seat or office, and a 12% turnover tax. Model C: a genuinely skill-determined knowledge contest is arguably outside 'gry hazardowe', but the Ministry of Finance maintains a public blacklist of infringing domains and the downside is criminal, so take Polish counsel before charging Polish players.

subdivisions.name: Romania
subdivisions.detail: Licensing market, but the economics turned hostile in 2025. From 1 August 2025 the authorisation tax on online gambling rose from 21% to 30% of gambling revenues and the minimum annual authorisation tax rose to EUR 480,000 — a figure that alone disqualifies an early-stage product. ONJN leadership was reset in April 2025 and the regulator has since pursued repeated blacklisting of unlicensed sites and stated publicly that unlicensed 'counterparty betting' will be treated as regulated gambling requiring full authorisation. A centralised self-exclusion register is expected in 2026 (President's Order no. 79/2025); Order 33/2025 defines notifiable 'significant changes'. Regulator: Oficiul Naţional pentru Jocuri de Noroc (ONJN).

subdivisions.name: Spain
subdivisions.detail: NO PURE-SKILL EXEMPTION — SPAIN SAYS SO EXPRESSLY. Art. 3(a) Ley 13/2011 defines 'juego' as any activity in which money or economically valuable objects are risked on uncertain future results 'dependientes en alguna medida del azar', permitting transfer between participants, 'con independencia de que predomine en ellos el grado de habilidad, destreza o pericia de los jugadores o sean exclusiva o primordialmente de suerte, envite o azar'. Art. 2.2 excludes only games or competitions 'de puro ocio, pasatiempo o recreo que constituyan usos sociales' with no economically evaluable transfers, and excludes promotional combinations with random elements. 'Concursos' — offerings where participation requires an economic outlay and prizes are awarded, chance possibly combined with competency tests — is a defined category and one of the four general-licence types alongside apuestas, rifas and otros juegos. A general licence must be held before the matching singular licence can be sought; general licences are awarded through a public convocatoria, not on demand. The DGOJ was consulting on amendments to Ley 13/2011 as at July 2026 (SECONDARY). Regulator: Dirección General de Ordenación del Juego (DGOJ).
subdivisions.authority: Ley 13/2011, de 27 de mayo, de regulación del juego, Arts. 1, 2, 3, 9 (BOE-A-2011-9280, consolidated text fetched 14 Sep 2026); Real Decreto 1614/2011 on licences, authorisations and registers.

subdivisions.name: Sweden
subdivisions.detail: Model C has a clean statutory exit; Model B does not. Spelinspektionen states on its own player-facing guidance that 'tävlingar där vinnaren utses genom ett prestationsmoment, det vill säga utan inslag av lottning eller slump' — competitions where the winner is decided by a performance element, i.e. without any element of drawing lots or chance — are NOT covered by the Gambling Act and fall outside Spelinspektionen's jurisdiction altogether. Note the wording is strict: 'utan inslag av... slump' — WITHOUT chance, not merely predominantly skill. A randomly drawn question set arguably introduces exactly the 'inslag av slump' that defeats the exemption, so a Swedish Model C must use an identical fixed question set for all entrants. Other exemptions at 3 kap. 4-5 §§ Spellagen: free-to-enter games, private play between close connections, combination games in periodicals/radio/TV, and municipal non-profit lotteries. Model B requires a Spelinspektionen licence. An amending act, SFS 2025:767, exists — ITS CONTENT IS UNVERIFIED.
subdivisions.authority: Spellag (2018:1138), in force 1 January 2019; exemptions 3 kap. 4-5 §§; Spelförordning (2018:1475). Spelinspektionen guidance page 'När krävs det inte licens?' fetched 14 Sep 2026. Regulator: Spelinspektionen.

risks: MODEL B IS NOT A CLOSE CALL IN THE EU AND SHOULD BE DROPPED FOR THIS REGION. The entire US sweepstakes-casino structure rests on negating 'consideration' via a free alternative method of entry. No EU member state uses a consideration gateway, and France pre-empts the workaround in terms: Art. L320-1 CSI deems financial sacrifice established 'même si un remboursement ultérieur est rendu possible par le règlement du jeu'. Reasoning imported from a US analysis will produce the wrong answer here.

THE 5/7/10-SECOND TIMER IS A LEGAL DESIGN DECISION, NOT A GAME-FEEL DECISION. Every favourable Model C verdict in the EU — Germany, Austria, Netherlands, Sweden — depends on a skill-versus-chance test. Short timers on randomly drawn questions convert knowledge into reflex and draw-luck, which is precisely what pushes the analysis toward chance. Sweden's carve-out is strictest of all: it requires the absence of any 'inslag av slump', not merely that skill predominates. Fixed identical question sets, longer timers and larger samples per contest all buy legal ground; the current duel format spends it.

AN MGA LICENCE BUYS ESTABLISHMENT, NOT MARKET ACCESS — AND FOUNDERS ROUTINELY GET THIS WRONG. There is no mutual recognition of gaming licences in EU law. Malta's Art. 56A (Bill 55, 2023) shield drew a Commission letter of formal notice, and in Case C-440/23 the CJEU confirmed that a member state may prohibit online gambling licensed elsewhere, that contracts breaching such a ban are void, and that players may sue to recover their losses. Serving Germany, the Netherlands or Austria on a Malta licence creates a restitution liability equal to gross player losses, not a regulatory fine.

THE 'ENTRIES' WORD IN MODEL A IS AN UNEXAMINED TRAPDOOR. Model A is described as coins buying 'cosmetics/entries only'. If those entries admit a player to anything carrying a prize of money or money's worth, Model A is not a closed loop at all — it is Model C with a currency layer, and every Model C analysis applies. Define precisely what an entry buys before treating Model A as safe.

A SUBSCRIPTION CAN BE THE CONSIDERATION THAT CREATES GAMBLING. The MGA's own controlled-skill-game definition counts consideration 'whether in the form of a stake, a periodic subscription or the purchase of in-game items, which provides an advantage to the player'. If the Model D subscription grants extra expedition entries, higher stake tiers or any competitive edge in a prize event, Model D converts into Model C. Keep it strictly cosmetic and strictly severed from prize contests.

BELGIUM CAN CRIMINALISE MODEL A IF COINS BUY RANDOMISED REWARDS. The Belgian Gaming Commission's 2018 position treats paid virtual currency plus chance plus an item of value as illegal gambling under the Gaming Act of 7 May 1999, enforced by threat of criminal prosecution. No loot boxes, no gacha, no randomised paid rewards in the EU build.

THE EU HAS NOW WRITTEN 'SKILL IS NOT AN ESCAPE' INTO DIRECTLY APPLICABLE LAW. AMLR Art. 2(1)(12) defines a gambling service as one involving 'wagering a stake with monetary value in games of chance, INCLUDING THOSE WITH AN ELEMENT OF SKILL'. Art. 4 lets member states exempt low-risk gambling but expressly forbids exempting providers whose principal activity is online gambling. From 10 July 2027 a Model B or Model C FACT//DUEL is an obliged entity with full CDD at a €2,000 stake-or-winnings threshold (Art. 20(5)), counting linked transactions. Design the KYC and transaction-attribution stack for this now — retrofitting it is far more expensive.

SEVERAL REGIMES ARE MID-FLIGHT AND ANY OF THEM CAN INVALIDATE A LAUNCH PLAN WRITTEN TODAY: Germany's statutory GlüStV evaluation is due 31 December 2026; Austria's reform was notified to the Commission in August 2026 with a 1 January 2027 cut-off for unlicensed operators to exit and stay eligible; Finland's licensed market opens 1 July 2027; Ireland's remote gaming licences are not yet open; the Netherlands re-licenses its 2021 cohort on 1 October 2026; Malta's gaming tax changed on 1 October 2026; Spain was consulting on amendments to Ley 13/2011 in July 2026; and the Digital Fairness Act is on the Commission's Q4 2026 work programme with virtual currencies in scope. Re-verify every date before committing engineering or capital.

ROMANIA'S MINIMUM ANNUAL AUTHORISATION TAX IS REPORTED AT EUR 480,000 (from 1 August 2025), which on its own disqualifies Romania for an early-stage product regardless of the legal analysis. Several smaller markets carry similar fixed-cost floors. Licence economics, not licence availability, will determine the realistic EU footprint.

THIS IS A COMPLIANCE CHECKLIST, NOT LEGAL ADVICE. Every Model C verdict turns on a fact-specific skill-versus-chance assessment that only a national regulator or court can settle, and this analysis was assembled from public sources in one research pass. Local counsel is required in every market before money is taken — priority order: Germany, Ireland, Spain, Italy, Netherlands, Sweden, and France (to confirm the geo-block rather than to seek a route in).

jurisdiction: European Union / EEA — horizontal digital law (EU-level instruments plus flagged member-state divergence). Excludes the gambling-licensing question, which is NOT harmonised at EU level and sits with 27 national regulators.
headline: Under EU horizontal law the cliff edge is REDEEMABILITY, not staking: the moment a purchased coin balance can be turned back into money you are presumptively issuing electronic money (Directive 2009/110/EC Art 2(2)) and need an EMI authorisation — while everything up to that line (Models A, C, D) is lawful but carries four non-negotiable EU obligations that most game studios get wrong: VAT on coin sales from the first euro (CJEU C-472/24 Žaidimų valiuta, 5 March 2026), a 14-day refund right on UNSPENT coins that you cannot waive away, real-money price labelling on every coin-priced item (CPC Key Principles, 21 March 2025), and an EU legal/data representative because you are not established in the EU.

modelVerdicts.reasoning: MODEL A is lawful under every horizontal EU instrument in this lane, but it is NOT an unregulated 'just cosmetics' model. Four hard obligations attach the instant you take the first euro. (1) E-MONEY: coins are not electronic money because the EMD2 Art 2(2) definition requires monetary value 'issued on receipt of funds for the purpose of making payment transactions' AND 'accepted by a natural or legal person other than the electronic money issuer'. In Model A only FACT//DUEL accepts them and they never convert back to money, so both limbs fail. Keep it that way: the decisive trigger is redeemability (EMD2 Art 11 requires redemption at par value for real e-money), so never offer a cash-out, a refund of an unspent balance in money beyond the statutory withdrawal right, or a player-to-player coin transfer that a secondary market can price. (2) VAT: since CJEU C-472/24 the sale of in-game currency is a taxable electronically supplied service — no financial-services exemption under Art 135(1)(e) VAT Directive and NOT a multi-purpose voucher under Art 30a, so VAT is due on the full consideration at the moment of the coin sale (Art 73), at the consumer's member-state rate (Art 58). A non-EU seller has no EUR 10,000 threshold: register for non-Union OSS before the first EU sale. (3) WITHDRAWAL: the CPC Network's position is that in-game virtual currency is NOT itself digital content, so the Art 16(1)(m) CRD waiver does not cover it — a consumer can withdraw within 14 days and demand a cash refund of any UNSPENT coins. Build a refund path, not an 'all sales final' term. (4) PRICING/UCPD: every item priced in coins must ALSO show its real-money price at the undiscounted bundle rate, exact-amount coin purchases must be possible, and parental controls with real-money spending OFF by default are expected for any game not exclusively adult. None of this makes Model A unlawful; all of it makes an unmodified launch unlawful.

modelVerdicts.reasoning: MODEL B is the one model that breaks the horizontal perimeter, and it does so twice over before you even reach gambling law. (1) E-MONEY. Once a player's purchased coin balance is redeemable for cash or for prizes of monetary value, the two EMD2 Art 2(2) limbs start to close: value is stored electronically against a claim on the issuer, and redemption into money is exactly what EMD2 Art 11 regulates. A leading Belgian practitioner analysis puts it plainly — redeemability makes the currency bidirectional and 'risks a qualification as actual e-money'. That means authorisation as an electronic money institution from a national competent authority (Central Bank of Ireland, BaFin, DNB, CSSF, MFSA etc.), with initial capital, own-funds, safeguarding of client funds in segregated accounts, and passporting. Note the EBA has confirmed (Q&A 2022_6336) that 'acceptance' requires genuine transferability and voluntary acceptance of the instrument itself as a separate monetary asset, not merely receipt of funds on redemption — so a narrowly drafted, operator-only redemption MIGHT stay outside the definition, but this is a perimeter question no founder should decide alone. (2) PAYMENT SERVICES. Taking money from Player 1 into an escrow and paying it to Player 2 looks like execution of payment transactions or money remittance (Directive (EU) 2015/2366 Art 4(22), Annex I point 6). The CJEU narrowed this on 16 July 2026 in C-51/25 Betaal Garant Nederland: transfers of funds made only to deliver another, primary, non-payment service are not themselves a payment service, and a 'credit transfer' requires the intermediary to hold the payer's payment account. That helps, but commentators stress the ruling is fact-specific and expressly did NOT address money remittance. Holding named per-player balances is precisely what pushes you back inside. (3) AML. From 10 July 2027, Regulation (EU) 2024/1624 (AMLR) applies directly and makes providers of 'gambling services' obliged entities, with the first EU-wide definition covering wagering a stake of monetary value in games of chance 'including those with an element of skill'. Model B is squarely within it. (4) And then 27 national gambling regimes, which are outside this lane but where the sweepstakes-casino structure has been the specific target of 2025–2026 enforcement. Verdict: not launchable in the EU without regulated-entity status or a licensed partner acting as merchant/issuer of record.

modelVerdicts.reasoning: MODEL C is the cleanest money-play structure under horizontal EU law but its regulatory characterisation is genuinely open. What is SETTLED: (a) the entry fee is consideration for an electronically supplied service, VAT-able at the consumer's rate through OSS (C-472/24 logic applies a fortiori to a fee, and Art 58 VAT Directive is unambiguous); (b) if the entry fee is paid by card directly to you through an authorised PSP and the announced prize is paid out of your own treasury, you are not storing redeemable value, so EMD2 does not bite — this is the single design choice that keeps Model C outside e-money; (c) the CRD withdrawal right is manageable here because a contest entry is a service the consumer expressly asks to begin immediately, and the Art 16(1)(m)/16(1)(a) waiver flow (separate click, explicit acknowledgement of loss of the right, durable-medium confirmation under Art 8(7)) can be run properly; (d) after C-51/25 Betaal Garant a fixed prize paid from operator funds is a strong 'ancillary to the primary service' story for PSD2 purposes. What is UNSETTLED and why I will not call it lawful: the AMLR definition in force from 10 July 2027 captures wagering a stake of monetary value in games of chance 'INCLUDING THOSE WITH AN ELEMENT OF SKILL'. A 5/7/10-second timed trivia duel over a randomly drawn question set is not obviously a pure skill contest — the question draw is stochastic and the timer converts knowledge into a probabilistic race. Whether such a contest is a 'game of chance with an element of skill' (AMLR obliged entity, full CDD, FIU reporting, AMLA-supervised) or a skill competition outside gambling entirely has no EU-level answer and no case law. The fixed, pre-announced, entrant-count-independent prize pool is the single most helpful fact — it removes the pooled-stake character most national regimes key on — but it does not resolve the AMLR wording. Requires member-state counsel in each launch market; do not treat a favourable answer in one state as portable.

modelVerdicts.reasoning: MODEL D is lawful under EU horizontal law and is by a wide margin the lowest-risk monetisation for an EU launch: no stake, no prize, no stored redeemable value, therefore no EMD2, no PSD2 perimeter question, no AMLR. What still applies: (1) VAT — a subscription to a digital service supplied to an EU consumer is taxable at the consumer's rate under Art 58 VAT Directive; a non-EU-established seller must register for non-Union OSS before the first sale, with no EUR 10,000 threshold (that threshold in Art 59c is only for EU-established cross-border sellers). (2) CRD — Art 6 pre-contractual information, Art 8(2) 'order with obligation to pay' labelling on the confirm button, Art 9 14-day withdrawal on the initial subscription, and if you want immediate access you must run the Art 16(1)(m) waiver correctly: express consent + acknowledgement of loss of the right in a click SEPARATE from the buy click (the CPC Network is explicit that it cannot be the same click as 'buy'), plus Art 8(7) durable-medium confirmation. (3) UCPD — cancellation must not be harder than sign-up; dark-pattern cancellation flows are the exact target of the forthcoming Digital Fairness Act. (4) Auto-renewal notice and easy-cancellation rules are set NATIONALLY, not by the CRD, and diverge sharply (Germany, France, Italy). (5) Do NOT add the old EU ODR-platform link to your terms: Regulation (EU) No 524/2013 was repealed by Regulation (EU) 2024/3228 with effect from 20 July 2025 and the platform is dead; the link is now stale boilerplate. ADR information duties under Directive 2013/11/EU survive.
