checklist.item: Register for VAT non-Union OSS (or Union OSS if you incorporate in the EU) BEFORE the first EU coin/subscription sale
checklist.issuer: Tax authority of one chosen EU member state of identification (e.g. Irish Revenue, Dutch Belastingdienst); framework: Council Directive 2006/112/EC Arts 358a–369k
checklist.cost: No EU registration fee known; UNVERIFIED. Compliance-provider cost UNVERIFIED
checklist.prerequisite: Legal entity; decide member state of identification
checklist.notes: CRITICAL AND ROUTINELY MISSED. CJEU C-472/24 Žaidimų valiuta (5 March 2026) settled that selling in-game virtual currency for real money is a taxable electronically supplied service: no Art 135(1)(e) financial exemption, and the coins are NOT a multi-purpose voucher under Art 30a, so VAT is due on the FULL consideration (Art 73) at the moment the coins are sold, not when they are spent. For a non-EU-established seller there is no EUR 10,000 threshold — VAT is due from the first euro. Your displayed coin prices must be VAT-inclusive for consumers, and the rate varies by member state, so either absorb the spread or vary the price per country.

checklist.item: Collect and store two pieces of non-contradictory customer-location evidence for every EU sale
checklist.issuer: Council Implementing Regulation (EU) No 282/2011 Arts 24b, 24f
checklist.prerequisite: OSS registration
checklist.notes: Billing address, IP geolocation, card BIN country, SIM country. Retain 10 years. Your product is currently accountless and stores everything in IndexedDB — that gives you NO location evidence, so this is a real backend requirement, not paperwork.

checklist.item: Appoint a GDPR Article 27 EU representative in writing
checklist.issuer: Private appointment; details must be published and given to data subjects and supervisory authorities (Regulation (EU) 2016/679 Arts 13(1)(a), 14(1)(a), 27)
checklist.prerequisite: Confirm you have no EU establishment; identify a member state where your data subjects are
checklist.notes: Mandatory for any non-EU controller offering services to people in the EU (Art 3(2)(a)). The Art 27(2)(a) 'occasional processing' exemption is cumulative and effectively unavailable to a live consumer game that processes continuously. Appoint in a member state where a substantial share of your players are. This is SEPARATE from the DSA legal representative below — do not conflate them, though one vendor can often supply both.

checklist.item: Designate a DSA Article 13 legal representative and notify the Digital Services Coordinator
checklist.issuer: Digital Services Coordinator of the member state of designation; framework: Regulation (EU) 2022/2065 (DSA) Art 13 — DSA fully applicable 17 Feb 2024
checklist.appliesTo: A, B, C, D — only if you are an 'intermediary service' (see notes)
checklist.prerequisite: Scoping decision on whether you are a hosting service
checklist.notes: SCOPE FIRST, THEN APPOINT. Today FACT//DUEL is almost certainly outside the DSA: all state is local, there is no storage of user-provided information. The moment you add accounts you will store player-chosen display names, duel room codes and any chat — that is 'storage of information provided by a recipient', i.e. a HOSTING service under DSA Art 3(g)(iii), which triggers Arts 11–16 including the Art 13 representative (who can be held personally liable for your non-compliance). You are very likely NOT an 'online platform' under Art 3(i), because a 1v1 duel is not 'dissemination to the public' (making information available to a potentially unlimited number of persons) — interpersonal 1:1 communication is expressly outside. Consequence: the heavy Section 3 duties (Arts 20–28, including the Art 28 minor-protection duty) do not apply, and Art 19 exempts micro/small enterprises from Section 3 anyway. If you ever add public leaderboards with user-authored text, global chat, or user-generated question packs, you become an online platform and this analysis flips.

checklist.item: Complete a GDPR Article 35 Data Protection Impact Assessment before launching accounts or real-money play
checklist.issuer: Self-assessed; consult the lead supervisory authority under Art 36 if high residual risk. Each DPA publishes an Art 35(4) mandatory-DPIA list
checklist.prerequisite: Records of processing (Art 30); data map
checklist.notes: A DPIA is effectively unavoidable here. National Art 35(4) lists commonly mandate a DPIA for services likely to be accessed by children and for profiling/behavioural tracking. You have: a knowledge-game likely to appeal to minors, session/retention analytics, skill-based matchmaking, streak and spend mechanics. If Model B or C, add financial data and gambling-adjacent behavioural risk, which pushes it firmly into Art 35(3)(a).

checklist.item: Maintain Article 30 records of processing activities (ROPA)
checklist.issuer: Self-maintained; producible to any supervisory authority on request
checklist.prerequisite: Data map
checklist.notes: The Art 30(5) sub-250-employee carve-out is cumulative and does not apply: your processing is neither occasional nor risk-free. As a non-EU controller the ROPA must also be kept by your Art 27 representative.

checklist.item: Run a documented DPO-necessity assessment under Article 37(1)(b)–(c)
checklist.issuer: Self-assessed; if appointed, notify the supervisory authority (Art 37(7))
checklist.prerequisite: Scale estimate of monitoring
checklist.notes: The 250-employee number is in Art 30 only and has nothing to do with DPOs. The trigger is 'core activities' consisting of 'regular and systematic monitoring of data subjects on a large scale'. A retention/cohort analytics engine plus matchmaking plus spend telemetry across a consumer player base is exactly the fact pattern regulators treat as regular and systematic monitoring. Write the assessment down even if the answer is no.

checklist.item: Map a lawful basis to every processing purpose and stop relying on a single blanket consent
checklist.issuer: Regulation (EU) 2016/679 Art 6
checklist.prerequisite: Data map
checklist.notes: Art 6(1)(b) contract for account, duel delivery, coin ledger and payment; Art 6(1)(c) legal obligation for VAT records and (in Model B/C) AML records; Art 6(1)(f) legitimate interests for anti-cheat, collusion detection and fraud prevention (do a documented LIA); Art 6(1)(a) consent for analytics, marketing and any personalised offer. The existing opt-in cohort ping in lib/cohort-client.ts is already built consent-gated, which is the right shape — keep that discipline.

checklist.item: Implement ePrivacy consent for non-essential terminal-equipment storage
checklist.issuer: National implementations of Directive 2002/58/EC Art 5(3) (e.g. CNIL in France, Garante in Italy, DSK guidance in Germany)
checklist.prerequisite: Inventory of IndexedDB/localStorage keys
checklist.notes: Art 5(3) covers ANY storing of or access to information on the user's device, not just cookies — your IndexedDB profile store is in scope. Game-state persistence needed to deliver the service the user asked for is strictly-necessary and exempt; the analytics day-rows and anonId are not, and need prior consent. Note ePrivacy is a directive, so this is 27 slightly different rules; the German TDDDG and the French CNIL guidance are the strictest in practice.

checklist.item: Decide international-transfer mechanism for every US or non-EEA processor
checklist.issuer: European Commission adequacy decision of 10 July 2023 (EU-US DPF); or Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2021/914 SCCs
checklist.cost: DPF self-certification fee to US Dept of Commerce: UNVERIFIED
checklist.prerequisite: Vendor inventory (Cloudflare, Stripe, analytics, error tracking)
checklist.notes: STATUS AS AT SEPT 2026: the DPF is still valid. The General Court dismissed the annulment action in Latombe v Commission on 3 September 2025; Latombe appealed on 31 October 2025 and the appeal is pending before the CJEU as Case C-703/25 P, limited to points of law, with no hearing date announced as at mid-2026 and Microsoft granted leave to intervene for the Commission on 29 June 2026. The CJEU killed both predecessor frameworks, so DO NOT build a US-processor stack that only works if the DPF survives. Put SCCs plus a transfer impact assessment in place as a fallback in every US processor contract now.

checklist.item: Show the real-money price alongside every coin price, at the undiscounted rate
checklist.issuer: CPC Network (national consumer authorities coordinated by the European Commission), Key Principles on In-game Virtual Currencies, 21 March 2025 — Principles 1 and 2
checklist.prerequisite: Coin-to-euro reference rate per member state
checklist.notes: Legal basis cited by the CPC Network: UCPD Arts 6(1)(d) and 7, CRD Art 6(1)(e). The price must be the objective cost of buying the required coins IN FULL, without quantity discounts or promos, regardless of how the player actually obtained the coins. Principle 2 also tells you not to run several stacked currencies or force multi-step currency exchanges. Your current 0/10/25/50/100 stake ladder and Expedition POINTS tier are fine today, but the instant coins are purchasable you must not let points and coins interconvert in a way that obscures the euro cost. The Key Principles are SOFT LAW — expressly non-binding, and industry bodies (Video Games Europe, EGDF) have publicly disputed parts of them — but they are the stated enforcement posture of the authorities who would investigate you, and a live CPC action against Star Stable Entertainment AB was announced the same day.

checklist.item: Let players buy the exact amount of coins they need; never force an over-purchase bundle
checklist.issuer: CPC Network Key Principles, Principle 3 (legal basis: UCPD Arts 5, 8, 9)
checklist.prerequisite: Coin shop design
checklist.notes: The two named practices to avoid are (i) offering coins only in bundles that mismatch the price of purchasable content, and (ii) denying the player the ability to choose the amount. This is the single most common design pattern in the market and the CPC Network has singled it out as likely to distort economic behaviour. Design your shop with an arbitrary-amount option from day one — retrofitting it after launch is far more expensive than building it.

checklist.item: Build a 14-day withdrawal and refund flow for UNSPENT coins
checklist.issuer: Directive 2011/83/EU Arts 9–16; CPC Network Key Principles, Principle 5
checklist.prerequisite: Coin ledger that distinguishes spent from unspent balance
checklist.notes: THE SINGLE MOST COUNTERINTUITIVE ITEM IN THIS LIST. The CPC Network's stated position is that in-game virtual currency is NOT itself digital content, so you MAY NOT use the Art 16(1)(m) exemption to kill the withdrawal right on the coin purchase. Named practices to avoid: 'exempting the purchase of in-game virtual currency, which is not digital content, from the right of withdrawal' and 'denying consumers' right to withdraw... within 14 days for any in-game virtual currency that remains unused'. Practical build: track FIFO coin lots with purchase timestamps, and refund the unspent remainder of any lot younger than 14 days. For the CONTENT bought WITH coins, the Art 16(1)(m) waiver IS available — but only if the consent-plus-acknowledgement click is SEPARATE from the buy button and you send an Art 8(7) durable-medium confirmation. German case law has upheld properly-run waivers for virtual currency, so the position is contestable — but building the refund path is far cheaper than testing it.

checklist.item: Rewrite terms of service to remove unfair terms flagged by the CPC Network
checklist.issuer: CPC Network Key Principles, Principle 6 (legal basis: UCTD Directive 93/13/EEC Art 3(1) and (3))
checklist.prerequisite: Draft ToS
checklist.notes: Specifically named as terms to avoid: unilateral rights to cease/modify/withdraw purchased content or purchased virtual currency; terms denying or limiting statutory rights; unilateral removal of purchasable features players expected to persist; A UNILATERAL RIGHT TO CHANGE THE VALUE OF THE VIRTUAL CURRENCY; and banning/suspending accounts or confiscating purchased content with no way to contest. That currency-revaluation point directly constrains how you can rebalance a paid coin economy post-launch — design the economy knowing you cannot silently devalue coins people paid for. Also: DELETE any EU ODR-platform link from your template terms — Regulation (EU) No 524/2013 was repealed by Regulation (EU) 2024/3228 effective 20 July 2025 and the platform is switched off; the link is now misleading boilerplate. ADR disclosure duties under Directive 2013/11/EU survive.

checklist.item: Turn real-money spending OFF by default and ship functional parental controls
checklist.issuer: CPC Network Key Principles, Principle 7 (legal basis: UCPD Arts 5–8 and Annex I point 28)
checklist.prerequisite: Account system
checklist.notes: The CPC Network's explicit action point: 'by default disabling the possibility of spending real-world money in the video game if the video game is not exclusively limited to an adult audience'. It also says ANY game not exclusively intended for adults should expect a significant under-18 player base, and that age gates do NOT discharge your responsibility. Two further stings that bite this product hard: Annex I point 28 UCPD bans direct exhortations to children to buy; and the guidance treats high-spending 'whales' as themselves a VULNERABLE group likely to struggle with impulse control or gambling disorders, so a business model built on whale extraction is assessed against a stricter fairness threshold. FACT//DUEL's juice/streak/escrow loop is precisely the design vocabulary this principle is aimed at.

checklist.item: Choose and document an age-assurance method proportionate to the model
checklist.issuer: EDPB Statement 1/2025 on Age Assurance (adopted Feb 2025); European Commission age-verification blueprint / 'mini-wallet' (v1 14 July 2025, declared feature-ready 15 April 2026); Commission Guidelines on the protection of minors under DSA Art 28 (July 2025)
checklist.appliesTo: A, B, C, D — proportionate to risk; strictest for B and C
checklist.prerequisite: DPIA; decision on whether you are an 'online platform' under DSA Art 3(i)
checklist.notes: The EDPB's ten principles require the LEAST intrusive effective method and set five criteria — accuracy, reliability, robustness, non-intrusiveness, non-discrimination — and distinguish self-declaration, age estimation and age verification. Self-declaration is defensible for Model A/D; it is not defensible for Model B and is doubtful for Model C. The Commission mini-wallet is built on the European Digital Identity Wallet specs, piloting in Denmark, Greece, Spain, France and Italy, and is the direction of travel ahead of EUDI Wallet rollout by end-2026 — integrating against it is the strategically correct bet, but note that adopting the app is not itself a compliance discharge. Separately, GDPR Art 8 sets the age of consent for information-society services at a default of 16 with member states free to lower it to 13 — so the parental-consent age literally changes at the border (see subdivisions).

checklist.item: Contract an authorised PSP as merchant of record / acquirer and implement SCA
checklist.issuer: PSP authorised under Directive (EU) 2015/2366; SCA under PSD2 Art 97 and Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2018/389
checklist.prerequisite: Legal entity, bank account, KYB onboarding with the PSP
checklist.notes: Using an authorised PSP is how you stay OUT of the PSD2 perimeter for the money-in leg. Implement EMV 3DS2 and handle the soft-decline/step-up path or your EU conversion collapses. A merchant-of-record PSP can also carry the VAT/OSS burden — worth pricing against doing OSS yourself. PSD3/PSR STATUS AS AT SEPT 2026: politically agreed 27 November 2025, final compromise texts published 23 April 2026, NOT yet adopted or published in the Official Journal (expected H2 2026), with most substantive rules applying roughly 21 months after entry into force — realistically late 2027/2028. So PSD2 and the 2018/389 RTS are still the operative law for your launch; build to PSD2 and track PSD3, notably the merger of the payment-institution and EMI regimes.

checklist.item: Obtain a regulatory perimeter opinion on whether holding player balances makes you a payment institution or an EMI
checklist.issuer: National competent authority (e.g. Central Bank of Ireland, BaFin, DNB, CSSF, MFSA) — via counsel
checklist.appliesTo: B mandatory; C strongly recommended; A only if you ever add cash-out
checklist.prerequisite: Final product spec including the exact money-in and money-out flows
checklist.notes: THE DECISION POINT OF THIS WHOLE ANALYSIS. Two limbs of EMD2 Art 2(2) must both be satisfied for e-money: stored monetary value representing a claim on the issuer, issued on receipt of funds for making payment transactions, AND accepted by someone other than the issuer. The EBA (Q&A 2022_6336) says acceptance requires real transferability and voluntary acceptance of the instrument as a separate monetary asset. So: coins that only you accept and that never convert back to money are not e-money. Coins redeemable at par for cash almost certainly are — EMD2 Art 11 exists precisely to regulate that redemption. For the money-OUT leg, CJEU C-51/25 Betaal Garant Nederland (16 July 2026) helps: fund transfers made only to deliver a primary non-payment service are not themselves a payment service, and a credit transfer requires the intermediary to hold the payer's payment account. But the Court expressly did not address MONEY REMITTANCE (PSD2 Art 4(22), Annex I point 6), practitioners call the ruling fact-specific, and two further CJEU references are pending. Do not lean on Betaal Garant as a licence substitute.

checklist.item: If any payment instrument you issue is used within a limited network, notify at the EUR 1 million threshold
checklist.issuer: National competent authority; PSD2 Art 37(2); EBA Guidelines EBA/GL/2022/02 on the limited network exclusion, applicable 1 June 2022
checklist.prerequisite: Transaction volume monitoring instrumented in the coin ledger
checklist.notes: If you rely on the PSD2 Art 3(k) limited-network exclusion, Art 37(2) requires a notification to your competent authority when the total value of payment transactions over any period shorter than 12 months exceeds EUR 1,000,000. The EBA guidelines say the notification is filed once, with a fresh one if the information changes substantially. Instrument your coin ledger to measure this from day one — a threshold you cannot measure is a threshold you will breach silently.

checklist.item: Build AML/CFT capability for a 10 July 2027 start date if you pursue Model B or C
checklist.issuer: Regulation (EU) 2024/1624 (AMLR), directly applicable from 10 July 2027; supervised by national FIUs/supervisors and the new Anti-Money Laundering Authority (AMLA)
checklist.appliesTo: B mandatory; C to be determined by counsel
checklist.prerequisite: Identity verification, transaction monitoring and record-keeping infrastructure
checklist.notes: AMLR Art 2(1)(12) gives the FIRST EU-WIDE definition of 'gambling service': wagering a stake with monetary value in games of chance, 'including those with an element of skill', such as lotteries, casino games, poker and betting, provided at a distance by electronic means at the individual request of a recipient. Because it is a regulation, it applies directly in all 27 member states without transposition — no more forum-shopping the definition. Obligations include customer identification and verification, understanding the purpose of the relationship, and ongoing risk assessment. Whether Model C's paid-entry skill contest falls inside 'games of chance... including those with an element of skill' is unresolved and needs counsel per market. Specific CDD monetary thresholds for gambling: UNVERIFIED in this research pass.

checklist.item: Document a DAC7 scoping conclusion (likely out of scope) and keep it on file
checklist.issuer: Council Directive (EU) 2021/514 (DAC7), amending Directive 2011/16/EU; reporting to the tax authority of the member state of registration
checklist.appliesTo: A, B, C, D — assess, probably not report
checklist.prerequisite: Final product spec
checklist.notes: DAC7's four 'Relevant Activities' are exhaustive: rental of immovable property, personal services, sale of (tangible) goods, and rental of any mode of transport. Prize money and gaming winnings are not among them, and players in a duel are not 'Sellers' providing a personal service to a customer for consideration — nobody is being paid for a time- or task-based service rendered at another user's request. So on the current design, none of Models A–D triggers DAC7 reporting. WRITE THE CONCLUSION DOWN. It would change if you ever add a creator marketplace (user-authored question packs sold to other players), paid coaching, or any revenue-share payout to individual content providers — at which point you become a reporting platform operator with annual reporting. Confirm with a tax adviser against your chosen member state's implementation; there is no Commission guidance specifically addressing gaming prizes.

checklist.item: Confirm the AI Act does not apply, and re-test the conclusion if you add any AI
checklist.issuer: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act); national market surveillance authorities and the EU AI Office
checklist.appliesTo: A, B, C, D — currently not applicable
checklist.prerequisite: Code audit of the deployed build
checklist.notes: I searched the repository: there is no LLM or AI dependency in the shipped product (no OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, or ML inference in app/, lib/ or components/). The AI Act therefore does not currently apply and you should not build for it. TWO TRIGGERS TO WATCH. First, if you add AI-driven personalised offers, dynamic difficulty tuned to spending, or emotion/behaviour inference aimed at maximising stake size, you must test against the Art 5 PROHIBITED practices — Art 5(1)(a) manipulative or deceptive techniques materially distorting behaviour and causing significant harm, and Art 5(1)(b) exploitation of vulnerabilities including age — which have applied since 2 February 2025 and carry the highest fine tier. A gambling-adjacent product with whale-targeted personalisation is close to that line. Second, if you add AI-generated questions or a chatbot, Art 50 transparency duties apply. STATUS: the AI Omnibus was adopted by Council 29 June 2026, published in the OJ 24 July 2026 and entered into force 27 July 2026, deferring stand-alone Annex III high-risk obligations to 2 December 2027 and Annex I embedded high-risk to 2 August 2028. The Art 5 prohibitions were NOT deferred.

checklist.item: Confirm MiCA does not apply
checklist.issuer: Regulation (EU) 2023/1114 (MiCA); ESMA/EBA and national competent authorities
checklist.appliesTo: A, B, C, D — not applicable on current design
checklist.prerequisite: Confirm no DLT or blockchain in the coin ledger
checklist.notes: MiCA's crypto-asset definition turns on the value being transferable and stored using distributed ledger technology or similar technology. A centrally-ledgered coin balance in your own database is not a crypto-asset and MiCA does not apply. Exact article reference and any in-game carve-out recital: UNVERIFIED in this research pass. This conclusion breaks immediately if anyone proposes putting coins on-chain or making them tradeable — at which point you would face BOTH MiCA and (for a redeemable coin) the e-money-token regime, which is the worst of all worlds.

checklist.item: Ship DSA baseline compliance if and when you become a hosting service
checklist.issuer: Regulation (EU) 2022/2065 (DSA) Arts 11, 12, 14, 15, 16; supervised by the Digital Services Coordinator of your member state of establishment or of your legal representative
checklist.appliesTo: A, B, C, D — only once accounts introduce stored user-provided information
checklist.prerequisite: Art 13 legal representative designated; DSA scoping decision made
checklist.notes: Baseline duties that apply to ALL intermediary services regardless of size (Art 19 does not exempt these): Art 11 single point of contact for authorities, Art 12 point of contact for users, Art 14 terms and conditions written clearly including your content-restriction policies, and — for hosting services — Art 16 notice-and-action mechanisms for illegal content. Art 15 transparency reporting also applies to hosting services. Because you are very likely not an 'online platform' (no dissemination to the public), Arts 20–28 do not apply, and Art 19 would exempt you from Section 3 anyway as a micro/small enterprise, with a 12-month grace period after you outgrow that status. Re-run this scoping if you add public chat, global leaderboards with user text, or user-generated question packs.

checklist.item: Track the Digital Fairness Act and design to its expected requirements now
checklist.issuer: European Commission (proposal expected H2 2026); not yet law
checklist.leadTime: Adoption unlikely before 2027; application later — all timing UNVERIFIED
checklist.prerequisite: Coin economy design decisions not yet locked
checklist.notes: COMMENTARY AND TRADE PRESS, NOT LAW. The DFA is trailed as a single instrument covering dark patterns, addictive design, loot boxes, virtual currencies, influencer marketing and unfair personalised pricing. Two expected provisions land directly on this product: an obligation to display the real-world monetary value of in-game purchasable items even when priced in virtual currency (which the CPC Key Principles already assert as current law), and possibly an outright loot-box ban or a parental-consent requirement for minors — the Netherlands is reported to be pushing for a full ban. Practical advice: if you build the real-money price display and the exact-amount coin purchase now, DFA compliance is close to free later; if you build a stacked dual-currency economy with randomised paid rewards, you are building a product you may have to dismantle. Treat every timeline claim here as unconfirmed press reporting.

checklist.item: Obtain member-state gambling counsel in every launch market before Model B or C
checklist.issuer: National gambling regulators (out of this lane)
checklist.prerequisite: Final product spec including stake mechanics and prize determination
checklist.notes: There is no EU gambling directive. Gambling is reserved to member states subject only to the TFEU free-movement rules (Arts 49 and 56) as policed by the CJEU, which permits national restrictions on public-interest grounds. That means 27 separate answers on whether a timed trivia duel for money is gambling, a skill competition, or a prize contest — and a favourable answer in Malta tells you nothing about Germany, the Netherlands or Poland. Horizontal EU law CANNOT resolve this and nothing in this checklist should be read as doing so.

subdivisions.name: All 27 member states — GDPR Article 8 age of consent
subdivisions.detail: The age at which a child can consent to an information-society service without parental authorisation is set at 16 by default but member states may lower it to any age down to 13. This is not a uniform number: your parental-consent gate must be country-aware, and a single hardcoded age will be wrong somewhere. Note this only matters where CONSENT is your lawful basis — for contract-based processing (Art 6(1)(b)) the relevant question is national contractual capacity of minors, which also varies.
subdivisions.authority: Regulation (EU) 2016/679 Art 8(1); national implementing laws

subdivisions.name: All 27 member states — gambling licensing
subdivisions.detail: Entirely outside harmonised EU law. Models B and C get a different answer in each state, and a licence or exemption in one confers nothing in another. Member-state counsel required per launch market. Out of this lane; flagged so it is not mistaken for a settled EU-level answer.
subdivisions.authority: Arts 49 and 56 TFEU; CJEU case law on national gambling restrictions; no EU gambling directive exists

subdivisions.name: All 27 member states — ePrivacy Art 5(3) implementation
subdivisions.detail: Because ePrivacy is a directive, consent rules for storing/accessing information on the user's device (your IndexedDB analytics state, not the strictly-necessary game state) are implemented and enforced nationally, with material differences in what counts as valid consent and how aggressively it is policed. France (CNIL) and Germany (TDDDG, DSK guidance) are the practical high-water marks.
subdivisions.authority: Directive 2002/58/EC Art 5(3) as amended by Directive 2009/136/EC; national implementations

subdivisions.name: All 27 member states — subscription auto-renewal and cancellation (Model D)
subdivisions.detail: The CRD does not harmonise auto-renewal notice periods, maximum initial terms, or cancellation mechanics for ongoing subscriptions — these are national rules and they diverge materially, with Germany, France and Italy among the most prescriptive. Several states require a specific easy-cancellation mechanism. Exact national provisions NOT VERIFIED in this research pass; obtain local counsel before launching Model D in any specific market.
subdivisions.authority: Directive 2011/83/EU does not cover this; national consumer statutes — specific sections UNVERIFIED

subdivisions.name: Denmark, Greece, Spain, France, Italy — age-verification blueprint pilot
subdivisions.detail: These five member states are the initial pilot for the Commission's age-verification 'mini-wallet', built on European Digital Identity Wallet technical specifications. Version 1 published 14 July 2025; the Commission declared the blueprint feature-ready on 15 April 2026, with EUDI Wallet rollout targeted before end-2026. If you need real age verification for Model B or C, these are the markets where a standards-based integration path exists first. Adopting the app is not itself a compliance discharge.
subdivisions.authority: European Commission age-verification blueprint (digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu); Commission Guidelines on protection of minors under DSA Art 28, July 2025

subdivisions.name: Sweden — CPC enforcement precedent
subdivisions.detail: The CPC Network's coordinated action announced alongside the Key Principles on 21 March 2025 targeted Star Stable Entertainment AB, a Swedish game operator, over direct exhortation to children in advertisements and time-limited pressure techniques in a virtual-currency economy. This is the live example of how the Key Principles are actually enforced — as a coordinated CPC action against a single operator, with commitments sought. Read it as the enforcement template for any coin economy aimed at or reaching minors.
subdivisions.authority: CPC Network coordinated action, announced 21 March 2025 (European Commission news release)

subdivisions.name: Netherlands — loot box and virtual currency posture
subdivisions.detail: Reported (trade press, not law) as pushing for an explicit loot-box ban in the forthcoming Digital Fairness Act, consistent with its historically aggressive national stance on paid randomised rewards. If your roadmap ever includes randomised paid rewards, treat NL as the strictest market and design to it. This is commentary, not verified law.
subdivisions.authority: Secondary sources / trade press only — UNVERIFIED

subdivisions.name: Member state of identification for VAT OSS — a real choice
subdivisions.detail: A non-EU seller registering for non-Union OSS picks ONE member state to file through and reports all EU digital sales in a single return. The choice determines your filing language, portal, audit relationship and practical support quality, and is worth deliberating rather than defaulting. No physical presence in the EU is required for the non-Union scheme. Registration fees and lead times: UNVERIFIED.
subdivisions.authority: Council Directive 2006/112/EC Arts 358a–369k (non-Union scheme); Art 58 place of supply

risks: REDEEMABILITY IS THE CLIFF EDGE, AND IT IS EASY TO FALL OFF BY ACCIDENT. Model A is safe only while coins are strictly one-way. A 'goodwill cash refund' policy for unhappy players, a tournament that pays winners in transferable coins, a player-to-player gifting feature that creates a grey market, or an account-closure policy that returns the unspent balance as money — any one of these can start to satisfy the second limb of EMD2 Art 2(2) and convert a games company into an unauthorised e-money issuer. Write the no-cash-out rule into the product spec and the terms, and make it a code-level invariant with a test.

VAT IS OWED AT THE COIN SALE, NOT AT THE SPEND — AND THIS BREAKS NAIVE FINANCIAL MODELS. C-472/24 (5 March 2026) means you owe destination-country VAT on the full consideration the moment coins are bought, before the player has consumed anything. Combined with the CPC position that unspent coins remain refundable for 14 days, you can be liable for VAT on a sale you later have to reverse. Model the cash-flow and build VAT-credit handling into the refund path.

THE 14-DAY UNSPENT-COIN REFUND RIGHT IS A FRAUD VECTOR IN A STAKING GAME. If a player can buy coins, stake and lose them, and then demand a refund, you have built a free-roll. The CPC position limits the right to UNSPENT currency, so the mitigation is a strict FIFO lot ledger that marks coins consumed at the moment of stake, plus clear disclosure. Get this architecture right before launch; it is close to impossible to retrofit onto a balance-only ledger.

DESIGNING FOR WHALES IS NOW EXPRESSLY A CONSUMER-LAW RISK, NOT JUST AN ETHICS QUESTION. The CPC Key Principles treat high-spending players as a VULNERABLE group likely to struggle with impulse control or gambling disorders, and say a business model based on targeting them is assessed under a stricter fairness threshold under UCPD Arts 5–9. FACT//DUEL's existing juice, streak, escrow and ceremony vocabulary is exactly the design language this is aimed at. A monetisation plan built on whale extraction is a UCPD exposure in the EU regardless of which of the four models you pick.

YOU WILL BE DEEMED TO HAVE CHILD PLAYERS WHETHER YOU TARGET THEM OR NOT. The CPC Network states that any game not exclusively intended for adults should expect a significant under-18 player base, and that age gates do not discharge the trader's responsibility to adapt its practices. A trivia game is the archetype of a product children reach. This drives the DPIA requirement, the Art 8 GDPR parental-consent gate, the spending-off-by-default expectation, and the Annex I point 28 UCPD ban on direct exhortation — all of which apply to Model A too.

THE EU-US DATA PRIVACY FRAMEWORK COULD FALL AGAIN MID-BUILD. It is valid today, but Latombe's appeal is live before the CJEU as C-703/25 P, the CJEU killed both predecessor frameworks, and a ruling is expected late 2026 or early 2027 — i.e. squarely inside your build-and-launch window. Do not design a US-processor architecture that has no fallback. Put SCCs plus transfer impact assessments in every US vendor contract NOW, and know which processors you could move to EU regions.

PSD3/PSR WILL RESHUFFLE THE PERIMETER RIGHT AFTER YOU LAUNCH. Political agreement 27 November 2025, compromise texts 23 April 2026, adoption expected H2 2026, most rules applying roughly 21 months later. The package merges the payment-institution and EMI regimes, which is precisely the perimeter Model B sits on. A structure engineered to sit just outside EMD2 today may be re-characterised under the new framework. Build Model B only with counsel who is tracking the PSR text, not the PSD2 text alone.

BETAAL GARANT IS A THINNER SHIELD THAN IT LOOKS. C-51/25 (16 July 2026) is genuinely helpful — ancillary fund transfers serving a primary non-payment service are outside PSD2 — but practitioners describe it as fact-specific and confined, it turned partly on the intermediary not holding the payer's payment account, it did NOT address money remittance, and two further CJEU references are pending. Holding named per-player balances is the fact most likely to defeat the ancillary argument. Do not let anyone treat this judgment as a licence substitute.

THE DIGITAL FAIRNESS ACT IS A KNOWN FUTURE RESET AND EVERY TIMELINE CLAIM ABOUT IT IS PRESS REPORTING. A proposal expected H2 2026 covering dark patterns, addictive design, loot boxes and virtual currencies will land on this exact product category. The cheap insurance is to build the real-money price display, the exact-amount coin purchase and the no-randomised-paid-rewards rule now, so that the DFA is a documentation exercise rather than a rebuild.

MODEL C'S AMLR CHARACTERISATION IS A REAL, DATED, UNRESOLVED EXPOSURE. From 10 July 2027 the AMLR's directly-applicable definition captures wagering a monetary stake in games of chance 'including those with an element of skill'. A timed duel over a randomly drawn question set is not obviously outside that. If it is inside, Model C means full customer due diligence, transaction monitoring and FIU reporting as an obliged entity — a materially different cost base from a games company. Resolve this with counsel before committing engineering to Model C, not after.

A SINGLE FEATURE CAN FLIP YOU INTO THE FULL DSA ONLINE-PLATFORM REGIME. Today you are probably not even an intermediary; with accounts you are probably a hosting service; with public leaderboards carrying user-authored text, global chat, or user-generated question packs you become an 'online platform' and acquire Arts 20–28, including the Art 28 minor-protection duty that the Commission's July 2025 guidelines flesh out. Put a DSA scoping gate in the product review process for any social feature.

THE CPC KEY PRINCIPLES ARE SOFT LAW AND PARTS OF THEM ARE GENUINELY CONTESTED. The document itself says it does not bind national authorities or the Commission and that non-compliance is not automatically unlawful; Video Games Europe and the EGDF have publicly said the Network introduced new legal theories; German courts have upheld properly-constructed withdrawal-right waivers for virtual currency. You could win an argument on the withdrawal point. But the Principles state the enforcement posture of the authorities who would open the file, and a CPC coordinated action is itself the punishment regardless of the eventual legal answer.

TODAY'S DEMO COINS ARE OUTSIDE ALL OF THIS — AND THAT IS A ONE-WAY DOOR. Footnote 2 of the CPC Key Principles expressly excludes in-game currencies obtainable solely through gameplay and not purchasable with real-world money. FACT//DUEL's current demo coins and Expedition points sit in that carve-out. The moment a purchase path exists, the entire consumer-law layer switches on retroactively for the design, not just for the new purchase flow — including the price-display and no-stacked-currency principles that constrain how points and coins may relate to each other.

jurisdiction: India (Union of India — central law; Promotion and Regulation of Online Gaming Act, 2025 (Act 32 of 2025) + Promotion and Regulation of Online Gaming Rules, 2026, both operative from 1 May 2026)
headline: India is the hard stop: s.5 of the Promotion and Regulation of Online Gaming Act 2025 (in force 1 May 2026) criminalises offering ANY game played for a stake in expectation of winning — expressly "irrespective of whether such game is based on skill, chance, or both" — and s.2(1)(j) counts purchased, non-cashable virtual coins as a "stake", so MODEL B and MODEL C are criminal offences in India (3 years' imprisonment, ₹1 crore fine, cognizable and non-bailable, with directors personally liable and the Act reaching operators outside India), while only MODEL A (strictly no player-v-player staking of purchased coins, no prize of value) and MODEL D (subscription) survive.

modelVerdicts.reasoning: Lawful ONLY in its pure form, and FACT//DUEL's current duel mechanic breaks it. The prohibition in s.5 bites on an "online money game", defined in s.2(1)(g) as a game "played by a user by paying fees, depositing money or other stakes in expectation of winning which entails monetary and other enrichment in return of money or other stakes". Model A as defined has the money-in limb but NOT the winning/enrichment limb, so it falls outside s.2(1)(g) and lands inside "online social game" in s.2(1)(i): a game that (i) does not involve staking or participation with expectation of winning monetary gain, (ii) "may allow access through payment of a subscription fee or one-time access fee, provided that such payment is not in the nature of a stake or wager", (iii) is offered solely for entertainment, recreation or skill-development. Note s.2(1)(i)(ii) is permissive, not an exhaustive list of lawful payments — the operative exclusion is (i), staking and expectation of winning. Rule 9 of the 2026 Rules (five-factor determination test, per secondary sources) turns on whether rewards or in-game assets "can be transferred, redeemed, monetised or used outside the game environment"; purely cosmetic, non-tradeable items with no external market sit on the permitted side. THREE CONDITIONS ARE LOAD-BEARING AND FACT//DUEL CURRENTLY FAILS THEM. (1) Purchased coins must never be staked player-v-player. The existing escrow duel — both players stake coins, winner takes the escrow — becomes an online money game the moment those coins are purchasable, because s.2(1)(j) defines "other stakes" as "anything recognised as equivalent or convertible to money and includes credits, coins, token or objects ... whether it is real or virtual, which is purchased by paying money directly or by indirect means", and winning coins is "other enrichment in return of ... other stakes". CASH-OUT IS NOT REQUIRED for this to be an offence. This is the single most important India finding. (2) The word "entries" in the model description is dangerous: coins buying entry to any contest with a prize of value converts Model A into Model C. Entries must be to prize-free play only. (3) No transferability, no gifting, no secondary market, no account trading. The current free product (coins minted free, not purchasable, not cashable) is safe because free coins are neither "purchased" nor "convertible to money"; the risk begins at the first rupee. If real money is introduced, the only defensible architecture is two hard-separated ledgers: purchased currency that can ONLY buy cosmetics and can never enter a competitive path, and a free, non-purchasable currency for duel stakes — and even then "by indirect means" in s.2(1)(j) is broad enough that bundling free coins with a cosmetic purchase re-taints them. Registration is not required (online social games are registrable voluntarily only), but a voluntary determination application to OGAI is available and is the only way to get a written classification.
modelVerdicts.authority: Promotion and Regulation of Online Gaming Act, 2025 (Act 32 of 2025), ss.2(1)(g), 2(1)(i), 2(1)(j) and 5; Promotion and Regulation of Online Gaming Rules, 2026, rule 9 (rule number from secondary sources — gazette text not obtained). Both in force 1 May 2026 (Rules notified 22 April 2026, Gazette of India ref CG-DL-E-22042026-271974).

modelVerdicts.reasoning: Flatly criminal. There is no sweepstakes doctrine, no "dual currency" carve-out and no "alternative method of entry" defence anywhere in Indian law — those are US constructs and they do not travel. Three independent reasons Model B is an "online money game" under s.2(1)(g): the user pays money for coins; the coins are "other stakes" under s.2(1)(j) because they are "purchased by paying money directly or by indirect means" and are "real or virtual"; and the user plays "in expectation of winning which entails monetary and other enrichment", which is satisfied both by cash redemption and by winning further stakes. The skill/chance distinction is statutorily abolished — s.2(1)(g) says "irrespective of whether such game is based on skill, chance, or both" — so the old Indian jurisprudence (rummy, fantasy sports) is dead for online play. Consequences: s.5 prohibits offering, and equally "aid, abet, induce or otherwise indulge or engage in the offering"; s.9(1) imposes up to 3 years' imprisonment or a fine up to ₹1 crore or both; s.9(4) makes a second conviction carry a MINIMUM 3 years (up to 5) and a minimum ₹1 crore fine (up to ₹2 crore); s.10 makes s.5 and s.7 offences COGNIZABLE AND NON-BAILABLE, so arrest without warrant and no bail as of right; s.11 makes every person in charge of the business, and any consenting or conniving director/manager/officer, personally liable; s.16 lets authorised officers enter and search "any place, whether physical or digital", arrest without warrant, and override access controls. ADVERTISING IS A SEPARATE OFFENCE: s.6 bans any advertisement that "directly or indirectly promotes or induces any person to play any online money game", punishable under s.9(2) with up to 2 years or ₹50 lakh or both (note: s.6 is NOT listed in s.10, so it is not cognizable/non-bailable — most commentary gets this wrong). FACILITATING IS A SEPARATE OFFENCE: s.7 bars any bank, financial institution "or any other person facilitating financial transactions" from processing payment for an online money gaming service, punishable under s.9(3) with up to 3 years or ₹1 crore. OFFSHORE OPERATION IS NOT AN ESCAPE: s.1(2) states the Act "extends to the whole of India and also applies to online money gaming service offered within the territory of India or operated from outside the territory of India", and the long title expressly targets services operating "from foreign jurisdictions". s.14 allows blocking notwithstanding s.69A of the IT Act 2000; 8,376 betting/gambling URLs had been blocked as of 28 March 2026, and on 29 July 2026 OGAI issued its first advisory directing app stores, cloud providers, ISPs, telcos, banks, social media intermediaries, OTT platforms and ad agencies to delist apps, block payments and pull ads. The practical enforcement route against a foreign founder is app-store removal, payment blocking and DNS/ISP blocking within days — not litigation.

modelVerdicts.reasoning: Unlawful, and the fixed announced prize pool does not help. s.2(1)(g) requires only (a) paying fees, depositing money or other stakes, and (b) an expectation of winning entailing monetary or other enrichment. A fixed entry fee is "paying fees"; an announced prize is the expectation of winning. Nothing in the definition turns on whether the prize pool varies with the number of entrants, on peer-to-peer versus house-banked structure, or on skill — s.2(1)(g) says "irrespective of whether such game is based on skill, chance, or both". Secondary commentary on the Act is explicit that "trivia/quiz contests that charge entry fees and distribute cash prizes are banned", alongside fantasy sports, rummy and poker. THERE IS EXACTLY ONE EXIT AND IT IS NOT REALISTICALLY AVAILABLE TO A TRIVIA APP: s.2(1)(g) carves out e-sports, and s.2(1)(c) permits a game that (i) "is played as part of multi-sports events", (ii) involves organised competitive events in multiplayer formats under predefined rules, (iii) "is duly recognised under the National Sports Governance Act, 2025, and registered with the Authority or agency under section 3", (iv) has its outcome determined solely by skill, (v) "may include payment of registration or participation fees solely for the purpose of entering the competition or covering administrative costs and may include performance-based prize money for the player", and (vi) "shall not involve the placing of bets, wagers or any other stakes by any person, whether or not such person is a participant". Limb (iii) is the killer: recognition under the National Sports Governance Act, 2025 (Act 25 of 2025) must be obtained FIRST, and the Rules require the Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports member to be present and concurring before OGAI can even process an e-sport determination. E-sport registration with OGAI is then mandatory (90-day target, certificate valid up to 10 years). A mobile trivia app is not a multi-sports-event discipline and will not obtain NSGA recognition. I am deliberately NOT calling this "licence-required", because there is no licence a founder can buy — treat the paid-entry contest as closed in India.
modelVerdicts.authority: Promotion and Regulation of Online Gaming Act, 2025 (Act 32 of 2025), ss.2(1)(c), 2(1)(g), 5, 9(1); National Sports Governance Act, 2025 (Act 25 of 2025) (recognition precondition in s.2(1)(c)(iii)); Promotion and Regulation of Online Gaming Rules, 2026, rules 12-14 (rule numbers from secondary sources). In force 1 May 2026.

modelVerdicts.reasoning: Expressly lawful — this is the one model the statute affirmatively blesses. s.2(1)(i)(ii) provides that an online social game "may allow access through payment of a subscription fee or one-time access fee, provided that such payment is not in the nature of a stake or wager". A recurring fee for features/cosmetics with no stake and no prize of value therefore sits inside the permitted category and outside s.5. Conditions: the subscription must not buy entry to, or advantage in, any prize-bearing contest; subscriber-only currency must not be stakeable; there must be no cash-out, no transfer, no external monetisation of anything the subscription unlocks (rule 9's reward-monetisation factor). Registration is NOT required — online social games are registrable voluntarily, and the Central Government has not, on the sources available, notified any category of online social game into mandatory registration. A voluntary determination application to OGAI is nevertheless the cheapest insurance available, because it produces a written classification; note rule 10(2) (per secondary sources) that a favourable determination for one provider does not carry across to another, and rule 11 that determinations hold only while the model is unchanged — any move toward staking is a "material change" that must be notified and will trigger reclassification. Tax and data obligations still apply in full: 18% GST on the subscription (OIDAR registration from the first Indian rupee if supplied from outside India), and DPDP Act 2023 s.9 child-data duties, which are the real engineering cost.
modelVerdicts.authority: Promotion and Regulation of Online Gaming Act, 2025 (Act 32 of 2025), s.2(1)(i)(ii) read with s.5; Promotion and Regulation of Online Gaming Rules, 2026, rules 9, 11, 12 (rule numbers from secondary sources); in force 1 May 2026. Tax: Integrated Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017 (OIDAR). Data: Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 (Act 22 of 2023), s.9; Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025, G.S.R. 846(E), 13 November 2025, rule 10.

checklist.item: DO NOT launch Model B or Model C in India — hard geo-block India for any staking or prize feature (IP geolocation + app store country availability + payment BIN/country checks + account country lock)
checklist.issuer: Self-imposed; enforced by Online Gaming Authority of India (OGAI), MeitY
checklist.prerequisite: None — this is the gating decision
checklist.notes: s.1(2) of the PROG Act reaches services "operated from outside the territory of India", so a US or EU entity serving Indian users commits the s.5 offence. s.11 makes directors personally liable. Geo-blocking must be real, not a terms-of-service disclaimer; OGAI's 29 July 2026 advisory went to app stores, cloud providers, ISPs, telcos and banks, so the realistic failure mode is overnight delisting and payment blocking, not a lawsuit.

checklist.item: Architect two hard-separated currency ledgers: PURCHASED currency (cosmetics only, never stakeable, never winnable, never transferable) and FREE currency (duel stakes only, never purchasable, no cash value)
checklist.issuer: Self-imposed; classified by OGAI under rule 9
checklist.prerequisite: Decision to monetise Model A
checklist.notes: This is the central India-specific engineering constraint. s.2(1)(j) makes purchased virtual coins "other stakes" whether or not they can be cashed out, so the existing escrow duel (both players stake, winner takes the pot) becomes an online money game the instant the staked coin is purchasable. Beware "or by indirect means" in s.2(1)(j): bundling free stake-currency into a cosmetic purchase, or granting it on subscription, arguably re-taints it. Also remove any gifting, trading or account-transfer path.

checklist.item: Remove or India-gate coin-purchase entry into Expeditions and any paid-entry event with a prize; points staking is fine only while points are non-purchasable and non-convertible
checklist.issuer: Self-imposed; classified by OGAI under rule 9
checklist.prerequisite: Ledger separation above
checklist.notes: "Coins buy entries" converts Model A into Model C if the entry leads to a prize of value. Expedition points as currently designed (minted by play, not purchasable, not convertible) are outside s.2(1)(j) because the definition requires the item to be both "recognised as equivalent or convertible to money" and "purchased by paying money directly or by indirect means".

checklist.item: File a voluntary determination / classification application with the Online Gaming Authority of India to obtain written confirmation that the product is an "online social game" and not an "online money game"
checklist.issuer: Online Gaming Authority of India (OGAI), attached office of MeitY, head office NCT of Delhi
checklist.cost: UNVERIFIED — fee is published on the OGAI portal; amount not confirmed
checklist.leadTime: 90 days from a complete application (statutory target, "as far as practicable"); the clock resets on each request for clarification
checklist.prerequisite: Final product spec, revenue model description, user safety features, grievance mechanism, terms of use
checklist.notes: Optional, not mandatory: registration of online social games is voluntary and no category has been notified into mandatory registration on the sources available as at 14 September 2026. Worth doing anyway — it is the only way to get a defensible written classification before spending on India. Secondary sources place determination at rule 9, application at rule 8/12, 90-day timeline at rule 10, certificate validity up to 10 years at rule 14(2). A favourable determination binds only your product (rule 10(2)) and only while the model is unchanged (rule 11).

checklist.item: Do NOT pursue e-sport registration unless the product is genuinely a multi-sports-event discipline
checklist.issuer: Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports (recognition) then OGAI (registration)
checklist.leadTime: UNVERIFIED — NSGA recognition must be obtained first and that time is excluded from OGAI's 90-day clock
checklist.prerequisite: Recognition under the National Sports Governance Act, 2025 (Act 25 of 2025)
checklist.notes: s.2(1)(c)(iii) makes NSGA recognition a precondition, and OGAI cannot make an e-sport determination without the Ministry of Youth Affairs and Sports member present and concurring. A trivia app will not clear s.2(1)(c)(i) ("played as part of multi-sports events"). Listed here only so the founder does not waste months on it.

checklist.item: Register for GST as an OIDAR supplier (Form GST REG-10) if the selling entity is outside India and takes money from Indian consumers
checklist.issuer: Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs (CBIC) / GSTN
checklist.cost: No government filing fee; professional fees UNVERIFIED
checklist.prerequisite: Foreign selling entity; any supply to an unregistered Indian recipient
checklist.notes: Mandatory from the first transaction — there is no turnover threshold for non-resident OIDAR suppliers. Rate 18% IGST on subscriptions and in-app purchases. Monthly return GSTR-5A due by the 20th of the following month. A supplier with no physical presence in India must appoint an Indian representative for compliance. If you sell exclusively through Apple App Store / Google Play billing the storefront may handle Indian GST — UNVERIFIED, confirm with each store before relying on it.

checklist.item: Register for GST (Form GST REG-01) if you incorporate an Indian entity
checklist.issuer: CBIC / GSTN
checklist.prerequisite: Indian entity incorporation, PAN
checklist.notes: 18% on subscriptions and cosmetic in-app purchases as an online service. Note the 40% GST slab applies to "online money gaming" on the full face value of deposits (from 22 September 2025, 56th GST Council) — there is no lawful way to use that slab now that s.5 bans the underlying activity, so treat 40% as a marker of how the state views the category rather than a business option.

checklist.item: Use an RBI-authorised payment aggregator; for a foreign merchant collecting from Indian users, use a Payment Aggregator – Cross Border (PA-CB) authorised entity, or route through app-store billing
checklist.issuer: Reserve Bank of India (RBI)
checklist.prerequisite: Entity and GST position settled
checklist.notes: Reserve Bank of India (Regulation of Payment Aggregators) Directions, 2025, dated 15 September 2025, consolidated and repealed the 2020 PA-PG Guidelines, the 2021 clarifications and the October 2023 PA-CB circular. Three categories: PA-O (online), PA-P (physical), PA-CB (cross-border). Indians paying a foreign merchant is the import/outward leg (Outward Collection Account); per-transaction cap ₹25 lakh. You do not need your own authorisation — you need an authorised partner. Separately, s.7 of the PROG Act criminalises any person facilitating payment for an online money gaming service, which is why Indian PSPs will refuse anything that smells of staking.

checklist.item: Build DPDP child-data compliance: age assurance, verifiable parental consent for under-18s, and a hard switch that disables behavioural tracking, profiling and targeted advertising for any child user
checklist.issuer: Data Protection Board of India / MeitY
checklist.appliesTo: A, B, C, D (and the current free product)
checklist.cost: Engineering cost; penalty exposure up to ₹200 crore for s.9 breaches and up to ₹250 crore for security-safeguard failures
checklist.prerequisite: Any processing of personal data of Indian users
checklist.notes: Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 (Act 22 of 2023) treats everyone under 18 as a child. s.9(1) requires verifiable parental consent; s.9(3) prohibits tracking, behavioural monitoring and targeted advertising DIRECTED AT children — an absolute bar, not a consent-waivable one. DPDP Rules 2025 (G.S.R. 846(E), 13 November 2025) rule 10 prescribes the verification mechanics, including DigiLocker-based verification of a parent's identity and the parent-child relationship. Phasing: rules 1, 2 and 17-21 from 13 November 2025 (Board constituted); Consent Manager registration from 13 November 2026; full substantive compliance from 13 May 2027. THIS IS THE BIGGEST NON-GAMING COST FOR INDIA: FACT//DUEL's existing cohort/retention/session analytics would be unlawful as applied to minors. The cheapest compliant answer is a genuine 18+ gate for India.

checklist.item: Publish a DPDP-compliant consent notice, appoint a contact for data-principal grievances, and stand up breach-notification and data-erasure workflows
checklist.issuer: Data Protection Board of India
checklist.prerequisite: DPDP gap analysis
checklist.notes: Itemised, plain-language notice; consent withdrawal as easy as giving it; erasure on withdrawal. Significant Data Fiduciary designation (DPDP Act s.10, DPDP Rules 2025 rule 13) brings audits, algorithmic due diligence and possible restrictions on transferring specified personal data outside India — unlikely at launch scale but re-test on growth.

checklist.item: If the product hosts ANY third-party content (chat, user profiles, user-submitted questions, leaderboard names), comply with IT Rules 2021 intermediary due diligence: publish rules/privacy policy/terms, appoint a Grievance Officer with Indian contact details, and meet the takedown and grievance timelines
checklist.issuer: MeitY
checklist.prerequisite: Determination of whether you are an "intermediary" at all
checklist.notes: Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021, as amended by the Amendment Rules, 2026 notified 10 February 2026 and effective 20 February 2026. A pure publisher app with no third-party content is NOT an intermediary — but it also has no s.79 safe harbour. The 2026 amendment shortens grievance resolution, imposes 3-hour takedown for certain categories, adds a Grievance Appellate Committee route with a 30-day user appeal window, and adds labelling/metadata duties for synthetically generated (AI) content — relevant if any questions, art or voice are AI-generated. IMPORTANT: do NOT build to the 2023 "online gaming intermediary" / self-regulatory body regime (rules 4A/4B). No SRB was ever designated, the operative provisions never came into force, and PROG Act s.18 gives the Act overriding effect.

checklist.item: Scrub all advertising, app-store listing copy, influencer briefs and affiliate contracts of anything that promotes or induces money gaming
checklist.issuer: OGAI / MeitY; Ministry of Information and Broadcasting
checklist.prerequisite: None
checklist.notes: s.6 is a standalone offence: making, causing to be made, aiding, abetting or inducing any advertisement that "directly or indirectly promotes or induces any person to play any online money game". Penalty under s.9(2): up to 2 years or ₹50 lakh or both; repeat offences carry a minimum 2 years and minimum ₹50 lakh under s.9(5). Note s.10 makes only ss.5 and 7 cognizable and non-bailable — s.6 is not. Affiliates and influencers are caught in their own right, so indemnities alone are insufficient. Language like "stake", "bet", "pot", "escrow", "winnings" and "cash out" in India-facing copy invites a suo motu determination even for a lawful product.

checklist.item: Rewrite terms of service to state that coins have no monetary value, are non-transferable, non-redeemable, non-refundable in cash, and confer no property right
checklist.issuer: Self-imposed; evidential before OGAI under rule 9
checklist.prerequisite: Ledger separation
checklist.notes: Rule 9's determination factors (per secondary sources) include whether rewards or in-game assets "can be transferred, redeemed, monetised or used outside the game environment". Terms are evidence, not a defence — the architecture has to match them. Also cover subscription auto-renewal disclosure and cancellation under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019 and the Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules, 2020.

checklist.item: Choose the entity route: Indian private limited company, or foreign entity selling into India with an OIDAR registration and Indian representative
checklist.issuer: Ministry of Corporate Affairs (MCA) for Indian incorporation
checklist.prerequisite: Confirmed classification as an online social game
checklist.notes: FDI in "gambling and betting" is a prohibited sector under India's FDI policy / FEMA Non-Debt Instruments Rules, so if the product were ever classified an online money game, foreign investment into an Indian operating entity would itself be unlawful — another reason to get the classification in writing before taking money. A lawful online social game is an ordinary digital service for FDI purposes (100% automatic route) — confirm with counsel against the current consolidated FDI policy.

checklist.item: Run a permanent-establishment / significant economic presence analysis before scaling India revenue
checklist.issuer: Central Board of Direct Taxes (CBDT)
checklist.leadTime: Before crossing India revenue or user thresholds
checklist.prerequisite: India revenue forecast
checklist.notes: Significant Economic Presence under s.9(1)(i) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 (Explanation 2A) creates a business connection in India for a non-resident above revenue or user thresholds prescribed by Rule 11UD of the Income-tax Rules, 1962. THE THRESHOLD FIGURES ARE UNVERIFIED in this research pass — do not plan against remembered numbers. Treaty relief may apply depending on the entity's residence. The 2% equalisation levy on e-commerce supply was withdrawn; confirm current position with counsel.

checklist.item: Obtain a written India opinion from Indian counsel before enabling any real-money flow, and re-test after the Supreme Court rules
checklist.issuer: Indian counsel (gaming/technology practice)
checklist.prerequisite: Final product spec and ledger architecture
checklist.notes: THIS IS A COMPLIANCE CHECKLIST, NOT LEGAL ADVICE. The points that genuinely need local counsel: (1) whether your specific purchased-coin design escapes s.2(1)(j)'s "indirect means"; (2) whether cosmetic loot boxes / randomised rewards survive rule 9 in OGAI's hands; (3) whether you are an "intermediary" for IT Rules purposes; (4) the FDI characterisation; (5) SEP/PE exposure; (6) whether an 18+ gate or verifiable parental consent is the cheaper DPDP path for your funnel.

risks: THE DECISIVE RISK: purchased coins staked player-v-player are an online money game EVEN WITH NO CASH-OUT. s.2(1)(j) defines "other stakes" to include "credits, coins, token or objects ... whether it is real or virtual, which is purchased by paying money directly or by indirect means", and s.2(1)(g) is satisfied by winning "other enrichment in return of ... other stakes". FACT//DUEL's core escrow duel therefore flips from lawful to criminal at the moment coins become purchasable. Founders coming from a US sweepstakes mental model consistently miss this.

Criminal, personal and non-bailable. s.10 makes ss.5 and 7 cognizable and non-bailable; s.11 makes anyone "in charge of, and responsible to, the company for the conduct of that part of the business" liable, plus any consenting/conniving director, manager, secretary or officer (independent and non-executive directors who are not in actual decision-making are carved out); s.16 permits entry and search of "any place, whether physical or digital", arrest without warrant, and overriding of access controls. This is not a regulatory-fine regime.

Extraterritorial reach is explicit. s.1(2): the Act "applies to online money gaming service offered within the territory of India or operated from outside the territory of India". The long title names services operating "from foreign jurisdictions". Incorporating in Delaware or Dublin does not put Models B or C outside the Act — it only changes the enforcement route to blocking, delisting and payment cut-off under s.14 and the OGAI advisory machinery.

Enforcement is fast and intermediary-led, not court-led. OGAI became operational on 1 May 2026 and issued its first advisory on 29 July 2026 to app stores, cloud providers, ISPs, telcos, banks, social media intermediaries, OTT platforms and advertising agencies, citing ss.5, 6 and 7. 8,376 betting/gambling URLs had been blocked as of 28 March 2026, over 4,800 of them after the Act. Expect removal from Indian app storefronts and payment refusal within days of a complaint, with the appeal happening afterwards.

The Supreme Court challenge is pending and there is NO stay. Head Digital Works v Union of India, T.C.(C) No. 133/2025, before a three-judge bench of CJI Surya Kant, J. Joymalya Bagchi and J. V.M. Pancholi; High Court petitions were transferred under Article 139A in September 2025; hearings ran through 2026 with a listing on 5 August 2026; no judgment found as at 14 September 2026. The Act came into force on 1 May 2026 notwithstanding the challenge. Plan on the Act standing; a favourable judgment would be upside, not a basis for launching now.

Classification can be revisited at any time. OGAI can determine suo motu (rule 9). Determinations bind only your product (rule 10(2), per secondary sources) and only while the model is unchanged (rule 11). Any move toward staking is a "material change" triggering reclassification, cessation directions, advertising prohibition and blocking (draft rule 13(4) machinery).

Social-casino and loot-box mechanics are the live policy debate. Indian commentary in 2026 openly describes cosmetic-currency games as exposing a "loophole" in PROGA — real money in, no cash out, casino psychology. MeitY can notify a category of online social games into MANDATORY registration at any time, and Rule 9's reward-monetisation factor gives OGAI a hook. A randomised-reward cosmetic economy in a game with duel framing is the highest-scrutiny design you could ship into India.

Oversight of social games is complaint-driven — which cuts both ways. There is no pre-clearance requirement, so you can ship without approval; but that also means a competitor, a parent or a consumer group can trigger a suo motu determination, and your first contact with OGAI will then be adversarial rather than a voluntary application you controlled.

DPDP's under-18 rules are a product constraint, not a policy document. Everyone under 18 is a child; s.9(3) absolutely prohibits tracking, behavioural monitoring and targeted advertising directed at children; penalties reach ₹200 crore for s.9 breaches and ₹250 crore for security-safeguard failures. The existing cohort/retention/session analytics and any personalised question-difficulty or ad targeting would be unlawful as applied to Indian minors. Compliance bites 13 May 2027.

App-store policy is a second, independent gate. Apple and Google separately restrict real-money gaming apps in India to licensed operators — and with PROGA there is no licence to hold. Even a lawful Model A/D build can be caught by over-broad store review if the listing copy uses staking language.

State gambling law and the Public Gambling Act, 1867 still exist for offline activity and some states (Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana) legislated against online gaming before PROGA. s.18 gives the PROG Act overriding effect to the extent of any inconsistency, but do not assume state-level exposure is fully extinguished without counsel.

Advertising liability attaches to people you do not control. s.6 catches anyone who makes, causes to be made, aids, abets or induces a money-gaming advertisement — affiliates, influencers, ad networks and celebrity endorsers in their own right. Contractual indemnities do not remove their criminal exposure or the reputational blast radius.
uncertain: I could NOT obtain the gazette text of the Promotion and Regulation of Online Gaming Rules, 2026. The G.S.R. number is UNVERIFIED (the PIB backgrounder gives the Gazette of India reference CG-DL-E-22042026-271974, dated 22 April 2026). All rule numbers I cite for the 2026 Rules (rule 9 determination, rule 10 timeline, rule 11 continuity, rules 12-14 registration and certificate, rule 16 point of contact, rule 17 data retention, rules 18-19 payment duties, rule 20 grievance, rule 23 safety disclosure, rule 26 registry) come from SECONDARY sources (Legal500 thought-leadership, Bar & Bench, gaganlegal, ipleaders, Mondaq) which are mutually consistent but which I could not check against the primary instrument. Treat every 2026 rule number as indicative. By contrast, EVERY section number and quotation from the Act itself is verified against the MeitY-published primary text of Act No. 32 of 2025, and the full text of the October 2025 DRAFT Rules is verified primary — but it is the draft, and the final Rules were restructured from 8 Parts to 6 Parts / 26 rules, dropped the Grievance Appellate Committee tier, moved certificate validity from 5 to 10 years, and changed registration from generally-voluntary-on-application to required-only-where-notified-or-for-e-sports.

OGAI registration and determination FEES: UNVERIFIED. Secondary sources say the fee is published on the OGAI portal; I could not retrieve an amount, and ogai.gov.in returned a 502 from this environment.

LEAD TIMES for incorporation, GST/OIDAR registration and PA-CB onboarding: UNVERIFIED. The only lead time I can state with confidence is the 90-day determination/registration target, and that clock resets on each request for further information.

Whether the Central Government has notified ANY category of online social game into mandatory registration: reported as none, but UNVERIFIED as at 14 September 2026. This is the single item most likely to change and should be re-checked immediately before an India launch.

Whether OGAI has issued any determination touching cosmetic-only in-app purchases, purchased virtual currency or loot boxes: I found NONE. The position for Model A therefore rests on statutory construction and commentary, not on regulator practice. This is genuinely untested.

The Act's commencement date. The MeitY-published compilation carries an internal inconsistency: the header records "President's assent & Gazette Notification, dated 22.08.2025", while footnote 1 reads "dated 22.9.2025". Every other source, including PIB, gives 22 August 2025 for assent; I have treated the footnote as a typographical error. Separately, s.1(3) left commencement to notification, and the Act was brought into force on 1 May 2026 by notifications issued 22 April 2026.

Supreme Court status. Head Digital Works v Union of India, T.C.(C) No. 133/2025 was pending as at the last case-tracker update I could retrieve (hearing listed 5 August 2026). I could not confirm whether judgment has since been delivered or reserved. Re-check before relying on any of this.

The reported Supreme Court decision of 27 May 2026 upholding 28% GST on online gaming rests on a SINGLE secondary source and I could not corroborate it. The separate 40% GST slab for online money gaming from 22 September 2025 (56th GST Council) is better corroborated but is commercially moot given the s.5 ban.

The precise GST rate and SAC classification for cosmetic in-app purchases as distinct from subscriptions: reported at 18% as an online service / OIDAR supply, but the exact classification is UNVERIFIED.

Whether Apple App Store and Google Play act as merchant of record and remit Indian GST for in-app purchases, and whether that removes the need for your own OIDAR registration: UNVERIFIED. Confirm with each storefront.
Significant Economic Presence thresholds under Rule 11UD of the Income-tax Rules, 1962: UNVERIFIED. I deliberately have not stated figures.

Whether the 2023 "online gaming intermediary" provisions (rules 4A/4B of the IT Rules 2021 and the self-regulatory body regime) have been formally omitted from the IT Rules, as opposed to merely never having been operationalised and now being overridden by s.18 of the PROG Act: UNVERIFIED. Practical effect is the same — no SRB was ever designated — but the formal status matters if anyone cites those rules at you.

A construction point worth counsel's attention: s.2(1)(j) reads "...which is purchased by paying money directly or by indirect means or as part of, or in relation to, an online game". On a narrow reading the relative clause "which is purchased" gates the whole definition, so free-minted coins are not "other stakes" (which is why the CURRENT free FACT//DUEL is safe). On an aggressive reading, "or as part of, or in relation to, an online game" is a disjunctive limb that could capture coins merely acquired in-game. The chapeau requirement that the thing be "recognised as equivalent or convertible to money" still protects free, non-convertible coins on either reading — but this is a genuine ambiguity and I have not found a determination or judgment resolving it.

checklist.item: Decide the product model BEFORE opening any merchant account, and never describe the business to a processor in terms that trip the prohibited list ('stake', 'wager', 'prize', 'cash out', 'escrow', 'winner takes the pot')
checklist.issuer: Internal / Stripe, Adyen, PayPal, Paddle underwriting
checklist.prerequisite: none
checklist.notes: Underwriting is done on your own copy. FACT//DUEL's current live UI already uses 'stake', 'escrow' and 'winner takes the escrow'. Those exact words map onto Stripe's prohibited line 'Payments of an entry or player fee that promise the entrant or player will win a prize of value'. Misdescribing the business is separately a termination-plus-clawback event under every processor agreement, so the fix is to change the product, not the wording.

checklist.item: Stripe standard account for coin purchases (closed-loop, non-redeemable) and for subscriptions
checklist.issuer: Stripe Payments Europe / Stripe Inc.
checklist.cost: 2.9% + $0.30 per successful domestic US card charge (stripe.com/pricing, fetched 14 Sep 2026); +1.5% international cards, +1% currency conversion
checklist.leadTime: UNVERIFIED (self-serve onboarding is same-day; underwriting review varies)
checklist.prerequisite: Legal entity, bank account, beneficial-owner KYC
checklist.notes: Lawful and supported ONLY while the coin is a true one-way closed-loop token: no cash-out, no redemption for anything of monetary value, no player-versus-player staking. Model A and D are ordinary digital-goods commerce.

checklist.item: Do NOT attempt Stripe for Models B or C — there is no pre-approval path
checklist.issuer: Stripe
checklist.prerequisite: none
checklist.notes: Stripe's Prohibited and Restricted Businesses list (last updated 13 May 2026) places in the PROHIBITED column: 'Games of chance including gambling, internet gambling, casino games, sweepstakes and contests, and fantasy sports leagues with a monetary or material prize'; 'Games of skill including video game and mobile game tournaments or competitions, darts, card games, and board games with a monetary or material prize'; and 'Payments of an entry or player fee that promise the entrant or player will win a prize of value'. That third line is a verbatim description of Model C. Stripe's own FAQ states it does not support gambling businesses 'regardless of local legality' and that the restriction extends to 'games of skill (or chance) with cash prizes, sweepstakes, pay-in auctions'. Restricted-list categories can be pre-approved; PROHIBITED ones cannot.

checklist.item: Adyen direct merchant account with written waiver for 'Legal gambling or Game of Skill'
checklist.issuer: Adyen N.V. (DNB/ECB banking licence)
checklist.cost: UNVERIFIED (Adyen is interchange++ with a per-transaction processing fee; no published gaming rate)
checklist.prerequisite: Gambling or skill-gaming licence in each target market; enhanced onboarding documentation; Adyen's written waiver
checklist.notes: Adyen's Prohibited and Restricted list (last updated 13 Nov 2025) marks 'Legal gambling or Game of Skill where participants receive cash or cash equivalents or prizes with/of material value: including but not limited to: Casinos, poker, bingo, slot machines, betting, lotteries, racing, fantasy sports' as RESTRICTED for direct merchants (waiver possible, revocable at Adyen's sole discretion) but PROHIBITED for platform/partner businesses. CRITICAL: 'Any type of US based gambling services' is in Adyen's PROHIBITED column outright — so Adyen is an EU/UK rail for Models B and C, never a US one.

checklist.item: Do NOT use Paddle or Lemon Squeezy for coin sales in any model
checklist.issuer: Paddle.com Market Ltd (Paddle owns Lemon Squeezy)
checklist.prerequisite: none
checklist.notes: Paddle's Acceptable Use Policy (last updated 13 April 2026) prohibits 'Virtual currency or stored value, including but not limited to store credit, gift cards, vouchers' — this kills even Model A's coin purchase, not just the gambling models.
